Lesson No. 95: At a Glance

As we said in the introduction to this surah, the whole surah is one unit. It is very difficult to divide it into separate lessons. This is like Surah al-An'am in the seventh para, about which we also gave the same opinion: every surah has its own temperament, its own personality and its own characteristics. The same is the case with this surah.

In this lesson, several matters of wisdom are mentioned, and they are mentioned as an explanation of the Book's attribute of wisdom. For example: the revelation of wahy to the Messenger of Allah, and why the revelation was sent down to a human being. Then it is explained how deep the wisdom is in the creation of the universe and in the physical system of the heavens and the earth: the sun was given intense light and the moon was given luminosity, and stations were determined for the moon so that people could keep count of months and years. Then the alternation of night and day and its wisdoms.

Lesson No. 95: Explanation of Verses 1 to 25

﴿Alif. Lam. Ra.﴾ The discussion of the disjointed letters (huruf muqatta'at) has already passed at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah (this is like the other disjointed letters).

﴿Tilka﴾: This word points to the verses of the surah or of the Qur'an.

Some have said: it points to the verses that were mentioned earlier in this surah.

﴿Tilka ayatu al-kitab al-hakim﴾: These are the verses of the wise Book. Al-Hakim is an attribute of al-Kitab: the wise, or the speech of the Wise One, or the firm and non-abrogated (muhkam ghayr mansukh). The latter meaning would apply when the verses refer only to the verses of this surah, since no verse in this surah is abrogated. If the whole Qur'an is meant, then "hakim" in the sense of "non-abrogated" cannot be said, since the rulings of some verses of the Qur'an are abrogated. Or, if "hakim" is taken in the sense of "muhkam", then it means that no verse in it is erroneous and there is no contradiction in its speech. Hasan said: In the verses of the Book, it is commanded to do justice and good, to give to relatives, to refrain from indecency, evil deeds and oppression, and there is Paradise for the obedient and Hell for the disobedient.

Ibn Jarir, through al-Dahhak, transmitted the statement of Ibn Abbas that when Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) as a prophet, the Arabs refused to accept him and said: "Would Allah send a human being as a messenger? His dignity is far above that." The following verse was then revealed:

1. Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas (رضي الله عنه) that "Alif. Lam. Ra." (i.e., the disjointed letters) are among the names of Allah that open the surahs.

2. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat, and Ibn al-Najjar in his History reported from Ibn Abbas (رضي الله عنه) that "Alif. Lam. Ra." means: "I am Allah, and I see."

3. Ibn al-Mundhir (رحمه الله) reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr (رحمه الله) that "Alif. Lam. Ra." means: "I am Allah, I see."

4. Ibn Abi Hatim (رحمه الله) reported from al-Dahhak (رحمه الله) that "Alif. Lam. Ra." means: "I am Allah, I see."

5. Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas (رضي الله عنه) that "Alif. Lam. Ra.", "Ha. Mim." and "Nun." are all separate names (i.e., this is one name that was split into separate letters), and that name is al-Rahman.

6. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas (رضي الله عنه) that "al-Rahim" and "Nun" contain the separated letters of the word "al-Rahman."

7. Abu al-Shaykh (رحمه الله) reported from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi (رحمه الله) that in "Alif. Lam. Ra.", the Alif, Lam and Ra are from the word "al-Rahman."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 2:

Is it a matter of wonder for the people that We have sent revelation to a man from among them? This is an interrogative of astonishment and denial (meaning: it is astonishing that people marvel at the fact that Allah sent revelation to a human being; they should not be astonished at this). The word lil-nas (for the people) indicates that the prophethood of a human being appeared to them as a marvel, something to be denied and mocked. A state that arises from witnessing an unusual event or observing something contrary to custom and habit is called ajab (wonder).

The reason the people's wonder is described in the verse as something that deserves astonishment, and their wonder is declared worthy of denial, is that the appointment of a human being as a prophet is not an unprecedented event. From the time of the creation of Adam (peace be upon him), it has been Allah's practice to always appoint human beings as prophets. Therefore Allah said: "And We did not send before you any but men" (Qur'an 12:109), meaning: We never sent before you anyone other than men as messengers.

It is the custom of kings that they adopt for their writing and speech the language known to the addressee, and the messenger is also sent from among the same kind as the people to whom he is sent. Benefit-taking and benefit-giving are not possible without suitability. For this reason Allah said: "Say: If there were in the earth angels walking securely, We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger" (Qur'an 17:95).

Ilā rajulin minhum (to a man from among them): that is, to an ordinary person who, in terms of worldly wealth and rule, is not among the great men. The disbelievers had said that if a human being was to be made a messenger, then other great people besides Muhammad (ﷺ) deserved to be made messengers. Allah (quoting this statement in these words) said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two cities?" (Qur'an 43:31), meaning: why was the Qur'an not sent down upon some great and mighty man from the two towns (Makkah and Ta'if). By "great man" they meant Walid ibn al-Mughirah of Makkah and Mas'ud ibn Amr al-Thaqafi of Ta'if. In refutation of this, Allah revealed: "Or do they distribute the mercy of your Lord?" (Qur'an 43:32), meaning: are they themselves distributing the mercy of your Lord, that is prophethood and messengership, so that they give it to whomever they wish? This was the folly of the disbelievers and their ignorance of revelation, for they considered entitlement to revelation and messengership to depend upon abundance of worldly wealth and tribal leadership. They did not regard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as a great man, although in every human quality and virtue other than wealth, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the greatest and most perfect of all. Lack of wealth has no bearing on prophethood; most of the prophets before you also passed in this same condition.

"That warn the people and give glad tidings to those who believe": that is, warn the people (of the evil consequences of disobeying Allah's commands) and give good news to the believers. He commanded warning all people in general, since very few people are there who do not deserve warning on account of their deeds. And since the disbelievers do not deserve glad tidings, the command to give glad tidings was restricted exclusively to the believers.

"That they have a sure footing (qadam sidq) with their Lord": that is, with their Lord they will receive their full rank.

According to Ata', qadam sidq means a station of truthfulness in which there is neither decline nor hardship or pain.

(According to the author) qadam sidq means an exalted rank towards which the believers are advancing and where they will remain. Rank is expressed by the word "foot" because the means of advancing and standing firm is the foot (i.e., the cause is mentioned for the effect), just as a favour is called a "hand," since favours are bestowed through the hand.

The word qadam sidq in the verse points to the fact that their elevated station with Allah will be attained solely through truthfulness of word and intention. And the truest statement is "There is no god but Allah." Our interpretation of qadam sidq as rank is also the essence of the interpretations of Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak. Ibn Abbas, explaining the word qadam, said: they will receive a good reward for the deeds they sent forward beforehand (a good reward and rank both mean the same thing). Al-Dahhak said: qadam sidq means the reward of truthfulness (al-Dahhak expressed rank through reward, and Ibn Abbas through a good recompense).

Hasan said: qadam sidq refers to the good deeds which the believers performed (before death); thus, according to Hasan, qadam means taqdim (advancement), that is, good deeds done in advance. By this word Allah gave the glad tidings that the good deeds the believers performed beforehand (i.e., before death) will be granted to them with Allah. Abu Ubaydah said: among the Arabs, everyone who advances is called qadam, whether towards good or towards evil. It is said, "So-and-so has qadam in Islam (precedence)," or "He has qadam with me," or "the qadam of evil," meaning, in my view he is advancing in goodness or in wrongdoing.

In one narration a statement of Ibn Abbas has come that qadam sidq means prior good fortune (sa'ada sabiqa). Zayd ibn Aslam said: it refers to the intercession of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Bukhari has recorded that Zayd ibn Aslam said: "for them is qadam sidq," that is, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (and his intercession).

"The disbelievers said": that is, when the disbelievers saw the miracles of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and heard his incomparable speech, they said out of mere obstinacy and stubbornness:

"Indeed, this is clearly a sorcerer." That is, indeed this (the claimant to prophethood) is a plain magician.

Surely your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth. (The truth is beyond doubt: your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth.) The heavens and the earth are the foundations of all possible beings (created things). According to the Greek philosophers, all things have come into being through their support and influence.

﴿in six days﴾: that is, within a period equal to six days of this world.

Allah could have created the whole universe in an instant, but in order to teach creation gradualness and deliberate progression, He created the heavens and the earth in six days.

﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾: then He settled (ascended) upon the Throne (the royal seat).

From the early generation to later ones, it is the unanimous belief of all the People of the Sunnah that Allah is free from all physical attributes and from the accidents of origination (ḥudūth). However, the aforementioned verse and similar verses (in which attributes of a body are apparently ascribed to Allah) appear to contradict the position and belief of the People of the Sunnah. To remove this doubt, two answers have been given:

(1) The path of ta'wīl (interpretation) has been adopted, that is, the (figurative) meanings of the apparent words that are fitting to the majesty of Allah have been taken. This is because in the verse ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾, "those firmly grounded in knowledge" is connected to "Allah." The meaning is that the true knowledge of the ambiguous (mutashābihāt) verses belongs to Allah and to those with firm knowledge (this shows that the scholars of divine knowledge (ʿulamāʾ rabbāniyyīn) also know the real meaning and interpretation of the ambiguous verses). The detailed discussion of this has already passed in Surah Āl ʿImrān. In the light of this explanation, in the verse under discussion, istawā has been taken to mean istawlā (to gain dominion). The meaning is that since the Throne, which is the highest and most elevated creation, is under Allah's control, Allah's dominion over the other creatures is obviously even more evident. Therefore, all creation is under His dominion. [(1) The meaning of istawā as istawlā and tasallaṭa (to dominate) occurs frequently in Arabic speech. A poet has a line:

"Bishr has gained (istawā) control over Iraq without wielding a sword and without shedding flowing blood."

That is, Bishr gained control over Iraq without drawing a sword and without shedding blood. (Translator)]

However, al-Baghawī said: To take istawā to mean istīlāʾ and tasallut (domination) is the view of the Muʿtazilah.

(2) The path of the righteous predecessors (salaf ṣāliḥ) is contrary to the path of the people of ta'wīl. All the scholars of the early generation have said that it is obligatory to believe in the apparent sense of such verses, that it is necessary to avoid probing and hair-splitting regarding them, and that it is necessary to entrust the knowledge of their reality to Allah. On this basis, Imam Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said that there is consensus among all jurists from the east to the west that it is obligatory to accept and believe in the attributes of Allah mentioned in the Qur'an and authentic ḥadīths, as they are (without elaboration, refinement or explanation). Whoever explains them acts against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the consensus of the predecessors. Such a person has no connection with the religion brought by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) or with the path adopted by the community of Muslims. Imam Mālik ibn Anas said: Istawā (its real meaning) is not unknown; its modality (kayfiyyah) is not known, and asking about the modality of istawā is an innovation (bidʿah).

The righteous predecessors affirmed the transcendence of the Lord (tanzīh), and along with that they accepted istawā ʿalā al-ʿArsh (the settling upon the Throne) without ta'wīl. Imam Abū Ḥanīfah said: Allah is certainly in the heaven, not in the earth. (Narrated by al-Bayhaqī.) It is also attributed to Imam Abū Ḥanīfah that whoever said, "I do not know whether my Lord is in the heaven or in the earth," has become a disbeliever, because Allah said: ﴿The Most Merciful settled upon the Throne﴾. And the Throne is beyond the heavens. There is also another saying of Imam Abū Ḥanīfah that whoever denies that Allah is in the heaven has become a disbeliever.

Imam al-Shāfiʿī said: Allah is upon His Throne in His heaven. He draws near to His creation as He wills, and He descends as He wills (meaning: Allah's being upon the Throne, His nearness to creation, and His descent are all three true statements, but the modality of being upon the Throne, of nearness to creation and of descent is not known). A similar statement is also narrated from Imam Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal.

Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh said: There is consensus among all the people of knowledge that Allah is established above the Throne and knows everything. Al-Muzanī, al-Dhahabī, al-Bukhārī, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah, Ibn Abī Shaybah, Abū Yaʿlā, al-Bayhaqī and other imams of ḥadīth hold this same view. From the statement of Abū Zurʿah al-Rāzī, it is clear that the consensus of the People of the Sunnah is upon this view. The scholar ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd al-Dārimī wrote that all Muslims agree that Allah is upon His Throne above the heavens. Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Tustarī said: It is not permissible to say, "How can One who created istawā be settled?" It is necessary for us to affirm and accept (istawā), because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said that Allah is upon the Throne. Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī wrote: It is sufficient for a Muslim to know that his Lord is settled upon the Throne. Whoever goes beyond this will be unsuccessful and a loser. Muḥammad ibn Khuzaymah said: Whoever does not say that Allah is settled upon the Throne above the seven heavens and separate from all creation is a disbeliever; he should be made to repent, and if he repents, well and good; otherwise his neck should be struck.

Al-Ṭaḥāwī wrote that the Throne and the Footstool (Kursī) are as Allah has described them in His Book. Allah is free from need of the Throne and of what is beneath the Throne. He encompasses everything and is above everything.

Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī al-Baṣrī, in his book Ikhtilāf al-Muḍillīn wa Maqālāt al-Islāmiyyīn, recorded a statement of the People of the Sunnah and the people of ḥadīth, the summary of which is that it is necessary to affirm belief in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers, and to acknowledge whatever word has come from Allah and whatever is mentioned in the authentic ḥadīths of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). None of these can be rejected. It is also necessary to affirm that Allah is upon His Throne, as He Himself said in the verse ﴿The Most Merciful settled upon the Throne﴾, and that Allah has two hands, but without modality (of creation). He Himself said: ﴿I created with My two hands﴾.

Abū Nuʿaym wrote in Ḥilyah: Our method is in accordance with the method of the predecessors, who followed the Book of Allah, the ḥadīths of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and consensus, and who believed that Allah has always been perfect in all His attributes... At the end, Abū Nuʿaym said: The predecessors affirmed the ḥadīths that mention Allah's being settled upon the Throne, and they affirmed that Allah is settled upon the Throne without any (creaturely) modality or resemblance, and they also held that Allah is separate from His creation.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr wrote that Allah is in the heaven, upon the Throne, above the seven heavens, as the People of the Sunnah maintain.

Al-Khaṭīb said: The method of the predecessors is to affirm such ambiguous verses, to take the words in their apparent meaning, and to negate modality and comparison (that is, no modality, illustration or resemblance should be stated. The meaning is known, but the modality of the meaning is unknown. We cannot liken the Face of Allah, the Hand of Allah, or istawā upon the Throne to the face, hand or sitting of creatures. These are attributes of Allah, but they are as is fitting to His majesty). Imam al-Ḥaramayn said: Following the belief of the predecessors is the preferred creed and the religion of Allah. The imams of the predecessors avoided ta'wīl, adopted the apparent meanings of the words, and entrusted the (elaboration and detail of the) meanings to Allah.

Al-Baghawī wrote: The People of the Sunnah maintain that istawā upon the Throne is an attribute of Allah, bila kayf (without modality). It is obligatory to believe in it. Al-Bayḍāwī wrote: Its meaning is that istawā upon the Throne is for Allah as is fitting for Him. It is free from any admixture of settling and locational place.

Abū Bakr ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā al-Shiblī, who was the greatest scholar among the Sufis of his time, said: The Lord is in the heaven; He commands and enforces His decree. Shaykh al-Islām ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī wrote in Akhbār Shattā that Allah is upon the Throne in the seventh heaven.

Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Jīlānī wrote in Ghunyat al-Ṭālibīn and discussed this subject in great detail (the summary of which is what has been transmitted from the scholars of the predecessors: the meanings are known, the modality is unknown, and it is free from every resemblance).

Al-Dhahabī has quoted all these statements in Kitāb al-ʿUlū. The major group of Companions, Successors, muḥaddithūn, jurists and Sufis (nearly all) hold this same view. I have explained briefly in the commentary of Surah al-Aʿrāf on the verse ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne; He covers the night with the day﴾, and in the commentary of Surah al-Baqarah on the verse ﴿Allah will come to them in clouds of shade﴾, that according to the people of the heart (aṣḥāb qulūb), a special manifestation (tajallī) and a particular radiance of the Essence of the Divine falls upon some creatures, and those creatures are illuminated by waves of light. This does not make the Essence of the Divine a locus of accidents, nor does it descend from pure transcendence to the level of resemblance. Rather, in contingent beings there arises a substance that becomes capable of receiving that radiance (the capacity for contingency and origination increases; within it the ability to receive manifestation grows and continues to grow). This outpouring of manifestation causes no change in necessity or eternity; the Essence of the Necessary and Eternal does not descend from necessity to possibility nor from eternity to origination. In the commentary of the verse ﴿Then He turned to the heaven and made it seven heavens﴾ in Surah al-Baqarah, I have clarified this outpouring of manifestation which occurs especially upon the heart of the believer, upon the Kaʿbah, and upon the Mighty Throne (that is, a special sphere of divine manifestation, through which a particular creature is illuminated by the manifestation of Allah). This does not necessitate that the One who pours out manifestation and light be in need of place or time, or be subject to qualities and quantities. That eternal manifestation is without modality... It is without place, without time, and every originated thing is free from magnitude and accidents.

﴿He arranges (yudabbiru) the affair﴾: He makes the (appropriate) arrangement of every matter. That is, in accordance with the demands of wisdom, He decides all the affairs of the universe. Tadbīr means to act while keeping in view the outcome of all affairs, so that the result is good.

﴿There is no intercessor except after His permission﴾: No one is an intercessor for anyone except after His permission. The greatness of Allah is expressed in this phrase. This verse was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, who said that if there were a Day of Resurrection, al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā would intercede for him. (Al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā were two idols in the form of women that were worshipped.) The verse hints that intercession will certainly take place on the Day of Resurrection, but only after Allah's permission.

﴿That is Allah﴾: That is, the Being who is the sum of the aforementioned attributes, and the aforementioned attributes require divinity; that very Being is Allah.

﴿your Lord﴾: That is, He alone is your Lord; there is no other lord besides Him, or there is no other partner in His attributes.

﴿So worship Him﴾: That is, do not worship anything other than Him. Inanimate objects aside, they have no capacity to benefit or harm; do not worship any human or angel either.

﴿Will you not then be mindful?﴾: Do you not reflect at all? Reflection should lead you to understand that Allah alone deserves worship, and that none of those you worship is worthy of being a deity.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 10, verse 4:

﴿إِلَيْهِ مَرْجِعُكُمْ جَمِيعًا﴾ (after death, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be raised to life and) all of you will return to Him. Is "marji'" a verbal noun (masdar) or a noun of place (zarf makan)?

﴿وَعْدَ اللَّهِ حَقًّا﴾ Allah has made a true promise. "Wa'da Allah" is a absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). ﴿إِلَيْهِ مَرْجِعُكُمْ﴾ is a promise from Allah, and the word "wa'da Allah" emphasizes this promise. "Haqqan" is also a maf'ul mutlaq and emphasizes the matter indicated by the word "wa'da Allah". Thus the first is a maf'ul mutlaq for emphasis of itself (ta'kid linafsihi), and the second provides emphasis of something other than itself (ta'kid bighairihi).

﴿إِنَّهُ يَبْدَأُ الْخَلْقَ﴾ Undoubtedly, it is He who originates creation. That is, it is He who gives this worldly life.

﴿ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ﴾ Then (after causing death, in the Hereafter) He will also give life again, a second time.

﴿لِيَجْزِيَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ بِالْقِسْطِ﴾ So that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice. In this case, "bil-qist" would mean justice from Allah. Or "qist" means that the believers are just and remain steadfast in justice in all matters. Or "iman" is meant, because faith itself is the greatest justice, just as shirk is the great injustice. Taking the latter meaning is more appropriate here, because the following verse mentions the requital of disbelievers for their disbelief (so it is more fitting that the preceding verse mentions the reward of the believers for their faith).

﴿وَالَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَهُمْ شَرَابٌ مِنْ حَمِيمٍ وَعَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ بِمَا كَانُوا يَكْفُرُونَ﴾ And those who disbelieved, for them will be a drink of boiling water and a painful punishment, as a requital for their disbelief. The flow of the expression clearly shows that disbelievers deserve punishment, and it also indicates the point that the primary purpose of the first and second creation is to give reward to the believers, while the punishment of the disbelievers occurs indirectly (as a by-product). Thus punishment is like a disease that arises from wrong belief and wrong deeds.

He it is Who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and ordained for it stages, that you might know the number of years and the reckoning. Allah did not create that except in truth. He details the signs for a people who know.

Note on the translation: "ضیاءً" is taken here as a radiance with an omitted noun before it, meaning "the essence" (ذات), so the phrase reads "the sun a radiance." Where the commentary says "ضیاءً قیام کی طرح مصدر ہے یا سیاط کی طرح جمع ہے" it refers to whether the word is a verbal noun like qiyam or a plural like siyat, with its singular being ضوء (ḍaw'), as سوط is the singular of سیاط (siyāṭ).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 6:

Verily, in the alternation of the night and the day (ان فی اختلاف الیل والنھار): "ikhtilaf" means one following another, coming and going, or it refers to the difference of colours, bright and dark.

And in what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth (وما خلق اللہ فی السموت والارض): and whatever creation Allah has made in the heavens and the earth, in it.

Are signs (لایٰت): clear indications of the existence of the Creator, of His oneness, of His perfect knowledge and power, and of His being free from every defect and imperfection.

For a people who fear (God) (لقوم یتقون): for those people who fear (the evil consequence), because this whole universe calls the people of taqwa (God-consciousness) to reflection and contemplation.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 10, verse 7:

Inna alladhina la yarjuna liqaa'na: Indeed, those who do not hope for meeting Us. Meeting here means reward, because the meeting with Allah and the vision of Him is the greatest reward.

Wa radu bil-hayat al-dunya: and they are content with the worldly life, that is, they have given preference to the worldly life over the life of the Hereafter.

Wa itmaannu biha: and they have settled down upon it. That is, they have come to rest in this life; its pleasures and adornments are their ultimate aim, and they have abandoned the deeds that will benefit them in the Hereafter.

Wa alladhina hum 'an ayatina ghafiluna: and those who are heedless of Our signs (of power and craftsmanship).

According to the translation above, the first alladhina will refer to the Jews and Christians, who acknowledge the existence of Allah and also hold the belief in resurrection and reckoning, but along with this they give preference to the world over the Hereafter and have despaired of the reward of the Hereafter. Their aim is only worldly enjoyment and comfort-seeking. The second alladhina refers to those who do not accept the Oneness of Allah and do not hold the belief in resurrection and recompense.

Baydawi has written: The first alladhina refers to those who deny the Hereafter; they have no hope of the reward of the Hereafter, and they know only this worldly life as life. The second alladhina refers to those whom the love of the world has made heedless of the thought of the Hereafter and preparation for it. According to some exegetes, both alladhina refer to the general disbelievers, but because of the multiplicity of attributes, a conjunction has been mentioned between them (as in "al-malik al-qarm wa ibn al-hammam wa laith al-katibah fi al-muzdahim": all these attributes, qarm, ibn al-hammam and laith al-katibah, refer to the king alone, but by treating the difference of attributes as a difference of persons, conjunctions have been placed between the attributes; in the same way, in the verses too, the multiplicity of attributes has been treated as the multiplicity of persons and conjunctions have been placed between them). There is also a warning in this matter that, since both groups possess and combine ugly attributes, they deserve the threat of punishment.

Baghawi has written: raja' means both fear and hope. On this reading, the meaning of the verse will be that they have neither fear of Our punishment nor hope of reward (that is, they have neither apprehension nor expectation of coming before Us).

Ibn Abbas said: 'an ayatina means, they are heedless of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an; they have turned away from them.

Those—their dwelling is the Fire, because of what they used to earn.

That is, because of their steadfast disbelief and their persistence in sins.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 10, verse 9:

Undoubtedly, those who believed and did righteous deeds, their Lord will guide them because of their faith. (It is) the guidance (to the path leading to Paradise) that their Lord will give them because of their belief.

Mujahid said: On the Bridge (Sirat), He will show them the path that leads them to Paradise. He will make a light for them by whose guidance they will go (to Paradise). Some said: By guidance is meant that, because of their faith, Allah will show them the path to understanding the realities of the religion. It is narrated from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever acts upon what he knows, Allah will grant him knowledge of what he does not know." Narrated by Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya. Some said: The meaning of yahdihim is that Allah will give them reward and recompense, or He will bring their aims to them within Paradise.

Baydawi wrote: Although the arrangement of the speech indicates that the cause of guidance is faith and righteous deeds (together), the explicit phrase "bi-imanihim" alone indicates that faith is an independent cause of guidance, while righteous deeds are its complement and completion.

"Tajri min tahtihimu al-anhar" – Rivers will flow beneath them. "Beneath" here means "in front of," as in the verse "Qad ja'ala Rabbuki tahtaki sariyya" where "tahtaki" means "in front of you," because Maryam sitting above the stream is not the intended meaning of that verse; rather, the stream being in front is meant.

"Fi jannat al-na'im" – In the gardens of bliss.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 10:

Their call therein will be: "Glory be to You, O Allah!" (Subhanaka Allahumma). They are those who are in Paradise, and in it their call will be to glorify You, O Allah; You are free of every evil, and we know and affirm You to be free of every defect and imperfection.

Baghawi has written: The people of tafsir state that between the people of Paradise and their attendants, the words "Subhanaka Allahumma" will serve as a sign of requesting food. When the people of Paradise desire food, they will say: "Subhanaka Allahumma," and immediately trays of their preferred food will be presented. Every tray will be one mil long and one mil wide. On every tray there will be seventy thousand bowls, and every bowl will contain food of a different color, no two resembling each other. After finishing the meal, they will all praise Allah. The meaning of "wa akhiru da'wahum an al-hamdu lillahi rabbil-'alamin" is this. Some scholars have said: the people of Paradise will say "Subhanaka Allahumma" with relish, meaning they will find pleasure in uttering these words.

Muslim, Abu Dawud and Imam Ahmad have related a marfu' hadith from Hadrat Jabir that the people of Paradise will be inspired by Allah to say "Subhan Allah" and "Al-hamdu lillah" as naturally as they breathe (meaning their tongues will involuntarily keep up glorification and praise).

"Wa tahiyyatuhum fiha salam": In Paradise, the first words their visitors address to them will be salam. One will greet another with salam, and the angels too will enter from every gate saying: "Salamun 'alaykum bima sabartum" (Peace be upon you for your patience). And angels will bring salam from Allah, saying: "Allah sends you salam" (that is, He gives you the good news of safety). Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Daraqutni and al-Ajurri related from Hadrat Jabir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: When the people of Paradise are occupied with their comforts, suddenly a light will shine upon them from above. They will lift their heads and see that Allah has manifested Himself to them from above. Allah will say: "Peace be upon you, O people of Paradise." This is the meaning of "Salamun qawlan min Rabbin Rahim."

Imam Ahmad, al-Bazzar and Ibn Hibban related from Hadrat Ibn Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Among Allah's creatures, the first to enter Paradise will be the poor emigrants (muhajirin), who manage the borders of Islam and through whom unpleasant matters are averted; yet when any of them dies, he carries his heart's desire within his heart, and he is not granted the ability to fulfil it. Allah will command whichever of His angels He wills to go to the muhajirin and convey His salam to them. The angels will submit: "O our Lord! We are the inhabitants of Your heavens, Your chosen servants among creation. Are You commanding us to go to them and greet them?" Allah will say: "These were My servants who worshipped none but Me and did not associate anything with Me. They were sent to the borders, and through them unpleasant matters were averted; and when any of them died, he died carrying his wish within his heart, without being granted the ability to fulfil it." By His command, the angels will come to them from every gate of Paradise and say: "Salamun 'alaykum bima sabartum, fa ni'ma 'uqba al-dar" (Peace be upon you for your patience; how excellent is the final abode).

"Wa akhiru da'wahum an al-hamdu lillahi rabbil-'alamin": And the last of their words (at that time) will be "Al-hamdu lillahi rabbil-'alamin." Perhaps the meaning is that when the people of Paradise enter Paradise and witness Allah's greatness, they will declare His majesty and manifest His attributes of glory. Then the angels will come from Allah and pray that they remain safe from all calamities and be honored and dignified. At that time they will praise Allah and speak of His attribute of bounty.

Baghawi has written: They will begin their speech with glorification and conclude it with "Al-hamdu lillah," and whatever they wish to say between these two, they will say.

Surah Yunus (10), verse 11, from the commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation):

"And if Allah were to hasten for people the evil [consequence], as they seek to hasten the good, their term would certainly have been decreed for them."

Ibn Abbas said: This refers to the kind of statement people commonly make in anger toward their family and children, such as "May Allah's curse be upon you" and similar words.

Qatadah said: The explanatory meaning of the verse is that when people make a supplication against someone, seeking swift evil, [the verse means]: if Allah were to respond to their curse with the same haste with which He responds to the good supplications of people. The verse mentions the hastening of the outcome for good supplications, but does not mention the swift granting of the outcome. And it does not mention "istijal" (seeking hastily) with evil, meaning it does not mention the swift seeking of the outcome with a curse, but mentions the swift granting of the outcome. In this way the speech became concise, and the unmentioned meaning became known from the context. It is narrated that Nadr ibn al-Harith (made a supplication against himself) and said: "O Allah, if this is the truth that has come from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky." Upon this, this verse was revealed.

"La-qudiya ilayhim ajaluhum": Then their term (of punishment) would long since have been fulfilled, meaning they would have been destroyed and died.

"Fa-nadharu alladhina la yarjuna liqa'ana fi tughyanihim ya'mahun": So We leave those who do not fear meeting Us [on the Day of Judgement] to wander bewildered in their rebellion (for some days, without punishment).

"La yarjuna liqa'ana," meaning: they do not fear the gathering (on the Day of Judgement) and the punishment. The "fa-nadharu" is connected to an implied sentence; the original sense was: but We do not hasten in destruction, and We do not destroy them immediately instead of granting respite, and We leave these disbelievers in misguidance to wander bewildered in their rebellion.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 10, verse 12:

When harm touches man, [وَإِذَا مَسَّ الْإِنسَانَ الضُّرُّ] he calls upon Us, lying on his side, or sitting, or standing. [Al-Dhurr means hardship and calamity.]

﴿دَعَانَا لِجَنبِهِ أَوْ قَاعِدًا أَوْ قَائِمًا﴾: he calls upon Us for deliverance, lying on his side (that is, reclining), or sitting, or standing. That is, in every state, whether lying, sitting or standing, he hastens to call upon Us to remove the calamity.

﴿فَلَمَّا كَشَفْنَا عَنْهُ ضُرَّهُ مَرَّ﴾: then when We remove his hardship and relieve him of it, he continues in his former way, persisting in disbelief and ingratitude.

﴿كَأَن لَّمْ يَدْعُنَا إِلَىٰ ضُرٍّ مَّسَّهُ﴾: it appears as though he had never called upon Us to remove the calamity that had touched him.

﴿كَذَٰلِكَ زُيِّنَ لِلْمُسْرِفِينَ مَا كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾: thus are the deeds of those who exceed the limits made to seem fair to them. That is, absorption in the desires of the self and turning away from remembrance and worship are made beloved in their eyes.

And We did destroy the generations before you when they committed wrong, (O people of Makkah!) and their messengers came to them with clear proofs, [but they would not believe]. Thus the proof was established against them and they became deserving of destruction. The same theme is stated in another verse, where He says: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾.

And they were not such as would believe: that is, they had no natural capacity to believe. The reflection of Allah's name al-Mudill (the One who leads astray) was their determined state, and therefore Allah also did not help them. Or the meaning is that they were not believers in Allah's eternal knowledge: Allah, even before creation, knew that they would die as disbelievers.

Thus do We recompense the guilty people. We give such punishment to guilty people: the punishment for those who deny the messengers and persist in disbelief is destruction, once it becomes certain that giving them respite will bring no benefit. Thus We shall give this same punishment to every guilty person, or to you. Crime itself demands this; crime makes one deserving of destruction.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 14:

ثم جعلنکم خلئف فی الارض من بعدھم
Then We made you successors in the land after them.

پھر ان کے یعنی ہلاک شدہ قوموں کے بعد ہم نے (اے اہل مکہ!) تم کو ان کا جانشین بنایا۔
Then after them, that is, the destroyed nations, We made you (O people of Makkah) their successors.

لننظر کیف تعملون۔
So that We may see how you act.

تاکہ ہم دیکھیں کہ تم کیسے عمل کرتے ہو اچھے یا برے اور گزشتہ اقوام کے احوال سے عبرت اندوز ہو کر پیغمبروں کی تصدیق کرتے ہو یا نہیں کرتے۔ یہ آیت بتا رہی ہے کہ اعمال و افعال بذات خود نہ اچھے ہوتے ہیں نہ برے۔ افعال کی اچھائی برائی ‘ کیفیت و جہت کے اختلاف پر مبنی ہے۔ ایک ہی عمل مختلف وجوہ کے تحت اچھا بھی ہوجاتا ہے اور برا بھی۔ حضرت ابو سعید خدری کی روایت ہے کہ رسول اللہ (ﷺ) نے فرمایا : دنیا میٹھی اور سرسبز ہے۔ اللہ تم کو یہاں (گزشتہ اقوام کا) جانشین بنائے گا اور دیکھے گا کہ تم کیسے عمل کرتے ہو۔
So that We may see how you act, whether for good or for evil, and whether, by taking warning from the conditions of earlier peoples, you confirm the Messengers or do not. This verse shows that actions are not good or bad in themselves; the goodness or badness of deeds depends on the difference of manner and aspect. One and the same act may become good under one set of considerations and bad under another. It is narrated from Hadrat Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The world is sweet and green. Allah will make you successors in it (in place of earlier nations) and will see how you act."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 15:

When Our clear verses are recited to them, [the ones] who do not hope for the meeting with Us say: "Bring a Quran other than this, or change it." Qatadah's view is that the reference is to the polytheists of Makkah. Muqatil said that this verse was revealed concerning five men: Mikraz ibn Hafs, Amr ibn Abdullah ibn Abu Qais al-Amiri, As ibn Amir ibn Hisham, Abdullah ibn Abi Makhzumi, and Walid ibn Mughirah.

Bayyinat (clear): that is, verses which plainly show that they have been sent down from Allah.

Qala alladhina la yarjuna liqa'na (they say, those who do not fear Our presence): that is, they do not fear the Gathering and deny the Resurrection.

I'ti bi-Quranin ghayra hadha (bring a Quran other than this): that is, bring another book, which we may read, and which does not contain matters that, in our view, are far from truth, such as reward and punishment after death, the prohibition of idol worship, and the exposure of their faults.

Aw baddilhu (or change it): that is, replace one verse with another verse. Muqatil reports that the five men mentioned above said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "If you wish us to believe in you, then present a Quran which is sent down from Allah, or not, in which there is no mention of the evil of Lat, Manat and Uzza and no prohibition of their worship. If such a Quran does not come from Allah, then make one yourself, or change this one, and give the command that the verse of punishment be replaced by a verse of mercy, and that the forbidden be made lawful and the lawful be made forbidden."

Qul ma yakunu li an ubaddilahu min tilqa'i nafsi (say: it is not for me to change it on my own accord): O Muhammad (ﷺ), say: it is not proper for me to change it on my own. In reply, only the changing of a verse (or of a command) is mentioned, and the bringing of another Quran is not mentioned, because when changing a verse is not possible, bringing another Quran is all the more impossible. Or it may be said that replacing one verse with another verse is within human capacity, whereas bringing another miraculous Quran like this one is beyond human power. So when a possible matter was denied, a matter beyond capacity was all the more denied. Or it may be said that by "ubaddilahu" is meant change in general: bringing another Quran in place of this one, or mentioning another verse in place of a verse (that is, I am not permitted any kind of alteration).

In tabi'u illa ma yuha ilayya (I follow only what is revealed to me): this sentence is the reason why he has no authority to change it. One who is merely a follower does not himself have any power of alteration or tampering.

In the Quran there are some verses which abrogate and some which are abrogated (and thus a change of verses takes place). The doubt that could arise from this is also removed by this sentence (that this change too is not of my own invention, but is revealed by Allah). The disbelievers, seeing the abrogating and abrogated verses, could have doubted that perhaps this is the words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) himself: when he wished he gave a command, and when he wished he abrogated it. The words "min tilqa'i nafsi" also refute this. The changing on his own account has been described in the next verse by the word disobedience.

Inni akhafu in 'asaytu rabbi 'adhaba yawmin 'azim (indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day): the great day means the Day of Resurrection. In this verse there is a hint that the disbelievers, because of the above-mentioned desire (that is, the request for a change of command and an alteration of the Quran), became deserving of punishment.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 10, verse 16:

Say: "If Allah had willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made it known to you through me." Or the meaning is: If Allah had not willed that this Qur'an be recited, He would not have sent it down to me.

"I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made you aware of it through my tongue."

"Indeed, I lived among you for a lifetime before it (i.e., for forty years) before the revelation of the Qur'an, and until revelation came to me, I did not state anything." This sentence points to the inimitability of the Qur'an. A person who lived among a people for forty years, who had not acquired any education, had not met any scholar, had never composed poetry, had never delivered a sermon, and then suddenly presented a book whose eloquence is superior to the eloquence of every speech and above every verse and prose, and in which all the principles of belief and action are mentioned, and in which past and future events are narrated accurately, then such a book cannot certainly be the fabrication of any creature; it can only be sent down by Allah.

"Will you not then use your reason?" Do you not reflect upon the Qur'an with your understanding and intellect, so that you would know that this book is not my fabrication but is from Allah?

Benefit: Until the age of forty, before revelation, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lived in Makkah. Then when revelation was sent down, he remained in Makkah for thirteen years after the descent of revelation, and after that he left Makkah and migrated to Madinah, where he resided for ten years. At the time of his death, the age of the Prophet (ﷺ) was 63 years. Related by Muslim from Ibn Abbas.

Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Salihi states that all scholars agree that after the Hijrah the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stayed in Madinah for ten years, and before revelation he lived in Makkah for forty years. However, how long he stayed in Makkah after prophethood is a matter of disagreement. The correct view is that he spent thirteen years in Makkah after prophethood.

Baghawi has transmitted the statement of Anas that after the beginning of prophethood the Prophet (ﷺ) remained in Makkah for ten years, and he passed away at the age of sixty.

Ibn Sa'd, Amr ibn Shaybah and al-Hakim, in al-Iklil, have also transmitted this same view through the narration of Ibn Abbas. Baghawi wrote that the first narration (that is, passing away at the age of 63 and remaining in Makkah for 13 years after prophethood) is both more well-known and clearer. Muslim transmitted from Anas that the death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) occurred at the age of 63, and that the age of Abu Bakr and Umar was also the same.

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi and Muslim, through the narration of Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, reported that the death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr and Umar occurred at the age of 63. The Two Shaykhs (Bukhari and Muslim), through the narration of Aishah, wrote that the death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) occurred at the age of 63. Nawawi declared this to be the sound and well-known view, and the consensus of the scholars.

Ahmad and Muslim wrote that Ammar ibn Abi Ammar reported: I asked Ibn Umar: "What was the age of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the time of his death?" He said: "Will you count it?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Forty, in which he was commissioned; he stayed in Makkah for fifteen years in a state of security and fear, and spent ten after the Hijrah in Madinah."

Hakim, in al-Iklil, through Ali ibn Abi Zayd, from Yusuf ibn Mihran, narrated that Ibn Abbas said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away at the age of 65." Hakim in al-Iklil and Nawawi wrote that according to the scholars, the most authentic narration by unanimous agreement is the one with 63 years; other narrations have been interpreted. The narration of sixty mentions only the tens, the units being disregarded. The narration of 65 is also open to interpretation or doubtful. Urwah rejected Ibn Abbas's narration of 65 years and declared it incorrect. Ibn Abbas did not witness the early period of prophethood. Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Salihi states that in most narrations the statement of Ibn Abbas is recorded as 63 years; it appears that Ibn Abbas initially mentioned death at 65, and then returned to the view of the majority (i.e., accepted death at 63).

Qadi Iyad mentioned, through Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, that the commissioning took place at the age of 43, but this report is shādh (anomalous); the correct age is 40.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 17:

﴿Who does greater wrong than one who invents a lie against Allah, or denies His signs? Surely the criminals will not succeed.﴾

Who does greater wrong than one who invents a lie against Allah and imagines that He has a partner and offspring?

Or denies His signs, that is, does not accept the truth of His verses and rejects them.

﴿Indeed, the criminals will not prosper.﴾ There is no doubt that the criminals, that is, the polytheists, will not attain falah (success), meaning salvation.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 10, verse 18:

﴿And they worship, besides Allah, that which neither harms them nor benefits them.﴾ The disbelievers of Makkah worship, besides Allah, things which, if they do not worship them, cannot harm their worshippers, and if they do worship them, cannot benefit their worshippers. That is, they worship idols which are completely lifeless, able neither to benefit nor to harm. A deity must have the power to benefit and harm, so that the one who worships it may receive its reward, be benefited, or have harm averted from him.

﴿And they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah."﴾ They say that these (deities) are our intercessors with Allah. They intercede for us in worldly affairs, and if there is a Resurrection, they will intercede for us there too.

﴿Say, "Do you inform Allah of something He does not know in the heavens or in the earth?"﴾ Say: Do you inform Allah of something that He does not know, neither in the heavens nor in the earth? That is, you are attributing a partner to Allah and claiming that there are other deities besides Allah. In this verse there is both a rebuke for the disbelievers and mockery (that you are such a great scholar that you inform of something which even Allah does not know). The words ﴿fi as-samawati wal-ard﴾ (in the heavens and the earth) point to this: whatever these people have made a partner of Allah, it would be one of the existents of the heavens, such as an angel, or one of the existents of the earth, such as a stone and so on; and the whole cosmos, heavenly and earthly, is entirely originated and subjugated. How, then, can it be correct to make it a partner in divinity?

﴿Glorified is He, and exalted above what they associate with Him.﴾ He is pure, and exalted above their associating partners with Him, or above the associators.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 10, verse 19:

وما کان الناس الا امۃ واحدۃ: "And mankind was not but one community." Meaning: all of them were monotheists, upon the fitrah (natural disposition) or upon Islam. The sense is that from the time of Adam until shortly before the mission of Nuh, or after the Flood, or from the era of Ibrahim until the time of Amr ibn Luhayy, all people were upon tawhid.

Or, "one community" means their unanimity in misguidance. The sense is that during the era of fatrah (the interval without messengers), all people were astray.

فاختلفوا: "Then they differed" (because of self-worship and following of desires, so that sects arose), or, after the sending of messengers, the misguided community split: one group followed the messengers and another group denied the messengers.

ولولا کلمۃ سبقت من ربک لقضی بینھم فیما فیہ یختلفون: "And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, the matter in which they differ would have been decided between them." The "word that preceded" refers to Allah's eternal decree that every community has a fixed term of life. Al-Kalbi said: the "word that preceded" means that Allah has promised to grant this community respite and not to destroy it with a worldly punishment. Liqudiya baynahum: that is, punishment would have been sent down in this world and the deniers would have been destroyed immediately, and this would have been the decision of their disagreement. Hasan said: Allah's eternal decision had already been made that before the Day of Resurrection, their differences would not be settled in this world in the form of reward or punishment, so that they would be admitted to Paradise or Hell in this world; rather, Allah has fixed the time of entry into Paradise and Hell for the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 10, verse 20:

Wa yaqooloona law laa unzila 'alayhi ayatun min rabbihi (They say: "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?")

Wa ya'qoolu... Hm, let me correct that: the quotation is in Urdu-style text, so I render the verse as the passage presents it.

﴿And they say, "Why has no sign been sent down upon him from his Lord?"﴾ — and the Quraysh of Makkah say: why was no sign (from among the signs we demanded) sent down upon him?

﴿So say: "The unseen belongs only to Allah. So wait; I too am among those waiting."﴾ — Say (O Messenger): the knowledge of the unseen belongs only to Allah; He alone knows why the demanded signs were not sent down and what the obstacle is. Or "the unseen" here means what is hidden from people, that is, the command of Allah which people do not know, and knowledge of it belongs to Allah alone.

﴿So wait.﴾ That is: wait for the descent of the demanded signs, or wait for Allah's judgment between us, to see which of us is upon the truth and which upon falsehood.

﴿Indeed, I am with you among those who wait.﴾ I too am waiting with you, watching what Allah does with you for denying the signs already revealed and for desiring new signs of your own choosing.

**Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah Yunus (10), verse 21:**

"When We let people taste mercy after some adversity has befallen them, behold, they begin to scheme against Our signs." When people are struck by some hardship and then We let them taste mercy, mercy here means greenness, cheapness of goods, plenty, and health; and adversity (ḍarrā') means drought, hardship, poverty and sickness.

﴿Idhā lahum makrun fī āyātinā﴾: immediately they begin to scheme against Our signs. Mujahid said: makr means denial and mockery. I say: makr means intending harm to someone secretly. Denial of the signs was, apparently, a denial of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a display of the intention to harm him; it was not a denial of Allah, yet the signs of Allah were in reality the word of Allah. Therefore, secret denial and the intention of evil return ultimately to Allah, and this is the reality of makr.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: Allah provided them with sustenance and sent rain, yet they did not believe that Allah was the Provider; rather they said: "Rain has come because of a star (nakshatra)." Their denial of the signs was this stratagem on their part, and this is what is called makr. It is also narrated that once the people of Makkah were afflicted with famine, then Allah had mercy on them and removed the famine. As soon as the famine was removed, they began to be ungrateful and to mock the signs of Allah. They did not give thanks for the blessing of Allah.

In a narration in Bukhari it is reported that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw the indifference and aversion of the disbelievers, he invoked a curse and said: "O Allah, help me against them by afflicting them with a seven-year famine like the seven years of (Prophet) Yusuf (peace be upon him)." As a result of this curse, a famine overtook the people of Makkah, so that everything (that is, crops, vegetables, fruits, etc.) was destroyed, and they reached the point of eating hides and carrion. Abu Sufyan came into the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ) and submitted: "Muhammad, your people have perished. You command us to obey Allah and to maintain ties of kinship (ṣilat al-raḥim). Pray to Allah for them, that Allah may remove their affliction." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made supplication. In another narration it is reported that after being afflicted with famine, the polytheists said: "O our Lord, remove this punishment from us, and we shall believe." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed (by Allah) that if this affliction were removed, these people would return to their original condition (and begin to disbelieve again).

In short, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made supplication, and Allah removed the affliction, but they returned (to polytheism and denial). Allah punished them for this on the day of Badr (by destroying the chiefs of polytheism).

﴿Qul Allāhu asra'u makrā﴾: Say: Allah is swifter in stratagem. His secret stratagem is either respite. 

Hazrat Ali has said: "If Allah expands someone's worldly life and he does not realize that this is respite from Allah, then his intellect is deluded." I say: the Hazrat's meaning is that a person who, after attaining expansion of worldly means, does not recognize Allah's respite and does not give thanks, is deluded.

Or makr means the punishment of makr, meaning: people devise secret plans afterwards, while Allah has already determined a secret plan of punishment for them, or a secret respite, before their conspiracies. Some have explained the swiftness of makr to mean that Allah devises the destruction of the disbelievers much more swiftly than the schemes they devise to repel the truth. Allah's punishment comes upon them very quickly. Since Allah has power, whatever He wills certainly comes to pass, and the disbelievers have no power to repel the truth.

﴿Inna rusalanā yaktubūna mā tamkurūn﴾: Indeed Our messengers (that is, the angels who keep watch over deeds) record what you scheme. The meaning is that your secret plots cannot remain hidden even from the angels who keep watch, so how could they remain hidden from Allah, who is the Creator of the whole universe?

He is the One who enables you to travel on land and sea. That is, He inspires you to journey and gives you the strength to move.

Until, when you are in the ships (and boats), ships (fulk) is used for one and also for more than one (so the word is both singular and plural). In this verse the plural meaning is intended, because the following clause refers to it with a plural pronoun.

And they sail with them, the ships (or boats) carry their passengers along. The address is in "you" (kuntum), and the pronoun in "bihim" is third person.

This shift in the wording was chosen to add force to the speech. The word "him" (هِمْ) shows that the discussion is not about the addressees but about other people whose condition is astonishing.

With a gentle wind, a breeze that carries them to their destination.

And they rejoice in it: they are glad because of the favourable breeze.

Then a violent wind comes upon them, that is, a fierce storm.

And waves come upon them from every place (or every direction).

And they assume that they are encircled: they become firmly convinced that they are surrounded on every side by waves and calamities, and there is no way of escape left. Signs of future destruction are present, and from signs one can only form a strong presumption, not certainty; therefore the word "thanna" (ظنوا) is used.

They call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion: at that time they all call upon Allah with pure conviction. That is, they supplicate Allah with sincerity of heart, and they call upon no one other than Allah. Even the polytheists of Arabia, when struck by severe hardship, used to call upon Allah alone.

"If You deliver us from this, we will certainly be among the thankful." That is, they say: if You deliver us from this... Or the meaning is that they call out: if You deliver us...

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 10, verse 23:

So when He delivers them, behold, they commit injustice on the earth without right. That is, when Allah accepts their supplication and grants them deliverance from the storm, at once they enter the bounds of corruption. Idhā (behold, suddenly) is for sudden occurrence, and baghy (transgression) means moving beyond the limits of what is permitted toward corruption. The phrase bi-ghayr al-haqq (without right) emphasises the meaning of yabghūn, since corruption is always without right.

A doubt might arise that the Muslims also destroy the settlements of the disbelievers, lay waste their fields and ruin their gardens, and that this too is corruption. To remove this doubt, it is said that these acts (which resemble corruption) committed by Muslims are not for destruction, but their purpose is construction and reform. They are done by the command of Allah, and the limits of what is permitted are not exceeded.

Yā ayyuhā al-nās innamā baghyukum ʿalā anfusikum: O people! (Know well that) this your transgression is a ruin (of your own souls) for you. The bad consequence of injustice returns to you yourselves. Al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mājah, with a ḥasan chain, narrated from the report of ʿĀ'isha that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: The good result of kind conduct and maintaining ties of kinship comes quicker than any other good deed, and the bad result of injustice and severing ties of kinship comes before the result of any other evil. Abu al-Shaykh, al-Khaṭīb and Ibn Mardawayh narrated in their tafsīr from the report of Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Three things return only upon the one who does them: injustice, deception, and treachery.

Ibn Lālī narrated from the report of Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: If a mountain oppresses a mountain, the oppressing one will split apart and be broken into pieces.

Matāʿ al-ḥayāh al-dunyā (the enjoyment of the life of this world): you enjoy it for a few days in worldly life, that is, it is temporary and perishing. Matāʿ al-ḥayāh is the object of an omitted verb, or of baghyukum.

Thumma ilaynā marji'ukum: Then (after death, or on the Day of Resurrection) your return is to Us alone.

Fa-nunabbi'ukum bi-mā kuntum ta'malūn: Then We will inform you of what you used to do, by recompensing your deeds (so that you know this recompense is for such-and-such a deed).

The unusual state of worldly life, that is, the worldly life is very quickly subject to decline. Despite this, people are infatuated with it; this is a strange matter.

ka-mā anzalnāhu mina as-samā'i: it is like the water which We send down from the sky.

fa-ikhtalaṭa bihi nabātu al-arḍi mimmā ya'kulu an-nāsu wal-an'ām: then, through this water, the plants of the earth, of which men and cattle eat, emerge thickly intertwined. Ikhtalaṭa means to become intertwined and dense. Mā ya'kulu an-nās means the food of men: grain, fruit and vegetables. Wal-an'ām means the fodder of the cattle: grass and feed.

ḥattā idhā akhadhati al-arḍu zukhrufahā wa-azyannat: until the earth had taken its full share of splendour and was thoroughly adorned. Zukhruf means beauty, splendour, the earthly loveliness produced by colourful flowers and vegetation.

wa-ẓanna ahluhā annahum qādirūna 'alayhā: and its owners supposed that they had full control over it.

That is, the owner of the land comes to think that now the produce of the land is in his possession; he can reap the crop and obtain grain, and pluck the fruit and benefit from it.

atāhā amrunā laylan aw nahāran fa-ja'alnāhā ḥaṣīdan (by some sudden calamity destroying the crop) by night or by day Our command arrives, and We make it like a harvested field. That is, We make the standing crop as though it had been cut down at the root.

ka-an lam taghna bil-ams: as if it had never flourished the day before. Lam taghna is derived from ghaniya bil-makān, meaning to stay, to dwell, to remain in a place. Bil-ams means shortly before this time, referring to the recent past.

This is a compound comparison to a compound. Although the thing being likened in the verse is water, the intention is to liken it to the whole course of the event. The whole theme is that the crops are green and the fruits of the garden are fresh, the earth is flourishing and full of splendour. The owners come to think that this produce and crop have escaped every calamity, and that no misfortune will now befall it; then suddenly the command of God arrives (through various earthly and heavenly calamities), and God reduces the lush gardens and verdant swaying crops to fragments and chaff. Such is the condition of worldly life. Qatādah said: God's command and His punishment come suddenly upon the person who trusts in the world and is immersed in its goods, while he is in a state of utter heedlessness. (Thus the reason for the comparison is heedlessness and carelessness, and the arrival of divine punishment in such a state.)

kadhālika nufaṣṣilu al-āyāti li-qawmin yatafakkarūn: Thus do We set out the signs clearly for a people who reflect.

God calls (people) to the Abode of Peace (Dar al-Salam), and He guides whom He wills to a straight path.

God is calling all people to an abode that is safe from every kind of ruin and destruction, that is, Paradise. Qatadah said: Paradise is the House of God. "As-Salam" is a name of God. That is, in the verse "as-Salam" does not mean peace; it refers to a specific name of God, and this is a form of attribute, not a verbal noun. The word "as-Salam" is mentioned to draw attention to this meaning.

Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sleeping when some angels came and said to one another: "Your companion has a particular condition; present an example and describe his state." One angel said: "He is sleeping." Another said: "His eyes are sleeping, but his heart is awake." Then the angels said: "His condition is like that of a man who built a house, set out a spread (table) for guests, and sent a man to invite the people. Those who accepted the invitation entered the house and ate from the spread, and those who did not accept the invitation did not enter the house and did not eat from the spread." (The other) angels said: "Explain this example so that this person may understand." One angel said: "He is sleeping." Another said: "His eyes are sleeping, but his heart is awake." The angels said: "Its explanation is that the house is Paradise, and the one who calls the people is Muhammad (ﷺ). Whoever obeyed Muhammad (ﷺ) obeyed Allah, and whoever disobeyed Muhammad (ﷺ) disobeyed Allah. People are divided into different groups." Related by al-Bukhari.

Al-Darimi also narrated this hadith through Rabi'ah al-Jurashi, but in that narration the words are: "It was said to me: a chief (of the people) built a house, prepared a spread, and sent a man to call (the common people) to eat. So whoever accepted the invitation entered the house, ate from the spread, and the host chief was pleased with him; and whoever did not accept the invitation did not enter the house, did not eat anything from the spread, and the chief was displeased with him." He said: "So Allah is the chief, Muhammad (ﷺ) is the caller, the house is Islam, and the spread is Paradise."

According to some scholars, in the verse "as-Salam" refers to the commonly known Islamic greeting of peace. The people of Paradise will greet one another with "salam" within Paradise, and that is why Paradise is called Dar al-Salam, and the angels will also greet them in Paradise. ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate: "Peace be upon you, for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the final abode!"﴾

﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾ The straight path means the religion of Islam, the way of the Sunnah, and the path that leads to Allah. The call is general (God is calling all people to Paradise), while guidance depends on the will of God. From this it is clear that there is a difference between the command (amr) and the will (irada). The command is directed to all people, while the will of guidance relates only to the believer. Allah (eternally) does not will to guide the disbeliever, although He has commanded the disbeliever to accept guidance as well. Deviation from the divine command is possible, indeed it occurs; most people act contrary to Allah's command, but no one can oppose Allah's will. Disbelief, like faith, occurs by Allah's will, but it is contrary to His command. This is the view of the Ash'arites. The Mu'tazilah do not distinguish between command and will; according to them, disbelief and every kind of sin do not occur by Allah's will.

Lesson No. 96 At a Glance

*Lilladhina ahsanu al-husna wa ziyadah*: For those who did good (in the world), there will be a good reward (in the Hereafter) and more (bounty) as well.

In explaining *ihsan*, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Ihsan (the excellence of worship) is that you worship Allah as though you see Him; and if you do not see Him, (then, if this station is not attainable, at least hold the certainty that) He sees you. (Reported in the Sahihayn from the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab.)

*Al-husna* means a good reward, that is, Paradise.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated on the authority of Ibn Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: *Lilladhina ahsanu* (means) those who bore witness that there is no god but Allah. *Al-husna* (means) Paradise. *Wa ziyadah* (means) looking at Allah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh have related the same saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the authority of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: On the Day of Resurrection, Allah will appoint a caller who will call out in a voice so loud that the first and the last will all hear it: O people of Paradise! Allah promised you a good reward and an increase. The good reward is Paradise, and the increase is attaining the sight of the Most Merciful.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Lalika'i and Ibn Abi Hatim have related a similar marfu' hadith from Ubayy ibn Ka'b through various chains. Ibn Mardawayh, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Lalika'i have related a marfu' hadith from Anas of the same meaning, and Abu al-Shaykh has also related a marfu' narration from Abu Hurayrah with the same theme.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh in their respective tafsirs, and al-Lalika'i, and also al-Ajurri in *Kitab al-Ru'yah*, have quoted the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Lalika'i and al-Ajurri have related the saying of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman under this verse to the same effect.

Hannad, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Lalika'i have also related the saying of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari to the same effect. Ibn Mardawayh, through the route of Ikrimah, has related the saying of Ibn Abbas in the same manner. Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Lalika'i, through the route of al-Suddi from Abu Malik from Abu Salih, have recorded the saying of Ibn Abbas, and on the authority of Ikrimah, the saying of Ibn Mas'ud to the same effect. Al-Lalika'i, through his chains, has attributed this same exegetical statement to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan al-Basri, Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, Amir ibn Sa'd al-Bajali, Ibn Abi Ishaq al-Subay'i, Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, Ikrimah, Mujahid and Qatadah.

Al-Qurtubi wrote in *Kitab al-Ru'yah*: This interpretation was widespread and well known among the Companions and the Successors, and such a consensus-based interpretation cannot be made without having heard it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Muslim and Ibn Majah have narrated on the authority of Suhayb that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: When the people of Paradise have entered Paradise, Allah will say: Do you desire anything more? They will say: Have You not made our faces bright? Have You not admitted us into Paradise? Have You not saved us from the Fire? (What more could we desire?) Then Allah will immediately lift the veil, and the people of Paradise will look at Allah. So at that moment, the most beloved thing given to them will be looking at Allah (that is, in comparison with the sight of Allah, all the blessings of Paradise will become insignificant). Al-Qurtubi has written: Lifting the veil means that all barriers to seeing Allah will be removed, and the people of Paradise will see with their eyes the light of His greatness and majesty just as He truly is. It is as though the veil is a veil for the creation (the creation cannot see Him here; it is a veil over their eyes), not a veil for the Creator (He is not hidden, rather there is a barrier over the eyes of the creation).

*Wa la yarhaqu wujuhahum qatarun wa la dhillah*: And neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces. Ibn Abi Hatim and others have related on the authority of Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud that *qatar* refers to dust in which there is blackness. *Dhillah* means disgrace, that is, unlike the people of the Fire, there will be neither dark dust nor humiliation upon the faces of the people of Paradise.

*Ula'ika ashab al-jannah hum fiha khalidun*: These are the people of Paradise, in which they will abide forever. The blessings of Paradise will neither decline nor will they ever perish.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 27:

Those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed shall be its like, and humiliation will cover them. Those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed shall be its like, and humiliation will cover them.

Alladhina kasabu (those who earned) is either conjoined to alladhina ahsanu (those who did good), or it is the subject (mubtada') with jaza'u sayyi'atin (recompense of an evil deed) as its predicate (khabar), or kaannama ughshiyat (as though they had been covered) is its predicate, or ula'ika ashabu al-nar (those are the companions of the Fire) is its predicate. Tarhaquhum means that it will cover them.

Ma lahum min Allahi min 'asim: they will have no one to protect them from the wrath of Allah. Min 'asimin contains an extra min (min za'id). Or: there will be no one who can protect them from the punishment of Allah.

Ka-annama ughshiyat wujuhuhum qit'an min al-layli muzliman: it will appear as though their faces have been covered with layer upon layer of dark night. Qita' is the plural of qit'a. Min al-layli qit'an is an explanation (bayan) of the preceding, and muzlimān is a circumstantial state (hal) from al-layl.

Ula'ika ashabu al-nari hum fiha khalidun: these are the people of the Fire; they will remain in it forever.

Objection: The Mu'tazilah hold that the perpetrator of major sins will remain in the Fire forever (that is, a believer who commits a major sin does not remain a believer). The Mu'tazilah have used this verse as evidence.

Reply: The word sayyi'at (evil deeds) applies to minor sins, to major sins, and also to disbelief. Now, if the general meaning of this word is intended, then the perpetrator of even a minor sin would have to be called an eternal inhabitant of the Fire, and no one holds that view. The words jaza'u sayyi'atin bimithlaha also testify against this opinion, because they show that the degrees of punishment differ: the punishment for a major sin is greater than that for a minor sin and less than that for disbelief. Necessarily, the reference of ula'ika cannot be generally to alladhina kasabu al-sayyi'at, but must point to some of those who committed evil deeds, namely only the disbelievers. Just as after wal-muṭallaqatu yatarabbaṣna bi-anfusihinna, the words wa-bu'ulatuhunna ahaqqu bi-raddihinna come, and the pronoun hunna does not refer to all divorced women in general (but to those women who were given a revocable divorce).

It is also possible that alladhina kasabu al-sayyi'at refers to disbelievers, because they are contrasted with alladhina ahsanu, and since faith is the summit of all good deeds, believers who commit major sins are also included among alladhina ahsanu. And when the perpetrators of major sins are included in alladhina ahsanu, then necessarily alladhina kasabu al-sayyi'at means only the disbelievers.

It is also possible that alladhina kasabu al-sayyi'at refers to the evildoers who existed during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because the believers who were in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were all Companions (sahabah), and the 'adalah (being free from sin) of the Companions is established by consensus (ijma'). If any Companion did commit some sin, he would immediately repent, and the sin would be forgiven by that repentance. One who repents of a sin becomes like one who has no sin, so we can say that in that era the sinners who committed evil were only disbelievers, and alladhina kasabu refers to exactly those people.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 10, verses 28–29:

And mention the Day when We shall gather them all together, that is, both groups.

Then We shall say to those who associated partners: "Stay in your place, you and your partners." Then We shall separate them from one another. The partners here refer to idols.

So We shall create a separation between them. That is, We shall sever their worldly ties and relationships, to the point that the false deities will express their disavowal of their worshippers. Or the meaning is that We shall separate them from the believers. A similar theme appears in another passage, where it is said: ﴿And stand apart today, O guilty ones﴾.

And their partners will say: "You did not worship us." The meaning is that We did not command them to worship us; they took us as deities on their own accord, without any warrant. God will, as it were, give the idols speech, and instead of interceding, they will express their disavowal of the disbelievers face to face. It has also been said that the partners here refer to angels and the Messiah. The Messiah and the angels did not command the polytheists to worship them, nor did they approve of this act of the disbelievers.

When the false deities speak as mentioned above, the polytheists will say: "Certainly not! We used to worship you." In response, the idols will say:

﴿So God suffices as a witness between us and you; we were certainly unaware of your worship.﴾ That is, God is a sufficient witness between us and you. We were indeed heedless of your worship; we neither heard, nor saw, nor understood it.

There, every soul will test what it sent forward. At that station, every person will examine the deeds they sent ahead and will see the benefit and harm of their past actions.

﴿And they will be returned to Allah, their true Master.﴾ That is, they will be returned to the judgment of Allah or to the punishment of Allah. The phrase ﴿mawlahumu al-haqq﴾ means that Allah alone is in reality their Master and the one responsible for their affairs; He is not the false deities whom the disbelievers took as gods.

An objection: the disbelievers have no mawla (protector), as Allah says: ﴿And that the disbelievers have no mawla.﴾
