Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 83:

So none believed in Musa except a small number of his people, out of fear of Pharaoh and their own leaders that he would persecute them. (Musa's miracles had defeated the sorcerers and he had presented the signs of truth.)

﴿Except a small number of his people.﴾ According to some commentators, the pronoun in "min qawmihi" refers to Musa. That is, only those Children of Israel who lived in Egypt and were with Musa when he left Egypt believed in him (the Copts did not believe).

Mujahid said: The believers were the descendants of those Israelites to whose guidance Musa had been sent. After their fathers had died, their sons remained. It is these people who are meant by "dhurriyyah" (offspring).

Some scholars said: When Pharaoh issued the order to kill the newborn sons of the Children of Israel, some Israelite women gave their newborn sons to Coptic women in exchange. These children were raised among the Copts, and on the day Musa overcame the sorcerers, these Israelites believed. (They were of Israelite lineage but outwardly Coptic.)

Some commentators say that the pronoun in "qawmihi" refers to Pharaoh. Ata'ibn Ata' reported from Ibn Abbas that a few people of Pharaoh's folk believed in Musa. Pharaoh's wife, Pharaoh's treasurer, the treasurer's wife, the maidservant who combed the hair of Pharaoh's wife, and the believer from the family of Pharaoh (mentioned in the verse of Surah Ya-Sin, "And there came a man from the farthest part of the city, running," [36:20]) were among these people, and these few believers are what is meant in the verse. (Narrated by Ibn Jarir.) In another narration from Ibn Abbas, it is said that they were seventy men whose fathers were Copts and whose mothers were Israelites. These people had followed their maternal relatives. Al-Farra' said: They were called "dhurriyyah" because their fathers were Copts and their mothers were Israelites, just as some Persians settled in Yemen and their descendants are called "Abna' Fars," because their fathers and mothers both came from another country.

﴿Out of fear of Pharaoh and their leaders that he would persecute them.﴾ The pronoun in "mala'ihim" refers to Pharaoh in the plural, for the sake of showing respect. Alternatively, "Pharaoh" here means his followers, that is, the Pharaonic people, just as "Rabi'ah" and "Mudar" refer to the tribes descended from Rabi'ah and Mudar. Or the pronoun refers to "dhurriyyah," meaning the believing offspring feared Pharaoh and their Coptic rulers. Or it refers to "qawm" (the people).

﴿And indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land, and indeed he was among the transgressors.﴾ There is no doubt that Pharaoh was lofty (powerful and arrogant) in the land of Egypt and was among those who exceed their limits, for despite being a created and needy being, he went beyond kingship and claimed lordship, and he had kept the sons of prophets as slaves and servants.

Musa said: "O my people! If you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him alone, if you are (truly) submissive (to Him)." (Musa said, seeing the believers in fear: "O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then put your trust in Him and rely upon Him (and do not fear Pharaoh and his men), if you accept (Allah's decision) and are sincere, then rely upon Allah alone.")

The condition for ان كنتم مسلمين (in kuntum muslimin) has its response omitted, and the response to in kuntum amantum is fa 'alayhi tawakkalu. Faith necessitates reliance upon Allah, so tawakkal (reliance) is connected with amantum. Until there is sincerity in the hearts and one surrenders one's being to the decree of Allah, the attainment of tawakkal cannot be achieved. Tawakkal is not attained by mixing one's own desires with the commands of Allah. Tawakkal is one of the stations (maqamat) of the Sufis.

Then they said: "In Allah have we put our trust." (Since those people were sincere and were true companions of the Messenger of Allah, they said: "Our trust is in Allah alone.") After this, they made supplication and said:

"Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people. Our Lord, do not make us a target of their oppression. Trial (fitnah) here means a target of punishment, the place where punishment descends. That is: O our Lord, do not give these wrongdoers power over us so that they may make us the target of their punishment. Or the meaning is: do not make us the cause of an increase in these disbelievers' disbelief and rebellion, so that we are directly afflicted by Your test, or so that punishment descends upon us at the hands of Pharaoh, and then Pharaoh's people say that if these people had been upon the truth they would not have been afflicted with punishment, and by this saying their disbelief and arrogance would increase."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 86:

﴿And deliver us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people.﴾ Meaning: deliver us from their deceit, their conspiracy and their ill omen.

Mentioning tawakkul (trust in Allah) before the supplication indicates that the one who makes du'a must first rely upon Allah, so that his du'a may be accepted.

I say: For the Sufi, tawakkul is among the qualities that must be present within him. Du'a, however, is not among the essential attributes but among the external accidents (if the Sufi makes du'a, it is better. The state of Sufism requires it, but it is not obligatory; and tawakkul is an obligatory distinguishing feature of the Sufi).

And We revealed to Moses and his brother (Aaron): "Settle your people in Egypt in houses, and make your houses into places of worship (qiblah), and establish prayer. And give good news to the believers."

That is, establish some houses, so that for residence and worship you turn away from all houses to the appointed houses.

Baghawi has written: Most of the exegetes state that previously the Children of Israel used to offer prayer only in churches and monasteries. But after the mission of Moses, by Pharaoh's order all places of worship were demolished, and the Children of Israel were forbidden to pray there. So Allah commanded the Children of Israel to build mosques within their own houses and to pray there. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i holds this same view, and in a narration from Ikrimah, this view is also reported from Ibn Abbas.

Mujahid states that Moses and his companions feared Pharaoh, lest, if they prayed in the congregational mosques, Pharaoh would have them seized and punished. Therefore Allah commanded that the Children of Israel build mosques in their houses, facing the Ka'bah, and pray there secretly.

"Make your houses a qiblah": by qiblah is meant a place of prayer that faces the qiblah, that is, that is situated upon the Ka'bah's direction. Ibn Jurayj has related the statement of Ibn Abbas that the qiblah of worship of Moses and his companions was the Ka'bah.

"And establish the prayer": so that the disbelievers, gaining dominance, do not cause them harm.

"And give good news to the believers": that is, O Moses, give the believers the good news that Allah will destroy their enemies and make them their successors in the land, and in the Hereafter will grant them Paradise. At the beginning of the discourse, Moses and Aaron were both addressed; then both were addressed together with their people, because the mosques within houses could be made through the efforts of both and with the counsel of the leaders of the people. And since it was obligatory for every person to appoint a place for prayer within the house and to perform the prayer there, all the believers were addressed. At the end, only Moses was addressed, because he was the bearer of the Shariah, and giving good news to the people was his duty.

Baghawi has written that the address "bashshir" (give good news) is directed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 88:

Musa said: "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment (زینۃ) and wealth in the life of this world, our Lord, so that they may lead astray from Your path." (Qur'an 10:88, partly)

By zīnah (adornment) is meant the means of adornment: clothing, jewellery, furnishings and furniture, household goods, means of transport, servants, attendants and the like.

Wa amwālan fi al-ḥayāt al-dunyā, Rabbanā li-yuḍillū 'an sabīlika: "and abundant worldly wealth in the life of this world, our Lord (with the result) that they lead astray from Your path."

The lām in li-yuḍillū is lām of consequence (lām al-'āqibah), that is, the lām which enters upon the outcome, such that what precedes the lām is the cause of what follows it. The meaning is that the result of Your giving was that they became misguided and misguiding. As another verse says: "Then the people of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief" (Qur'an 28:8). The people of Pharaoh found Musa, so that (as a result) he became their enemy and the cause of their grief.

Some exegetes have written that the lām here means "kay" (in order that), i.e., You gave them all this wealth and provision and granted them respite so that they would remain steadfast in misguidance. Or it may be said that since Pharaoh and his companions had made God-given wealth and status a means of misguidance, it was as though these things were given to them precisely so that they would go astray and lead others astray.

Rabbanā is repeated for emphasis, to express humility and intense supplication.

Shaykh Abu Mansur al-Maturidi said that Allah knew that the disbelievers would lead others away from Allah's path, so He gave them worldly wealth so that they would lead people astray through it (the purpose of giving wealth was, as it were, that they should go astray and lead others astray). As another verse says: "We grant them respite only that they may increase in sin" (Qur'an 3:178). In this case, this verse becomes clear evidence against the Mu'tazilah's position. The Mu'tazilah say that it is incumbent upon Allah to do what is most beneficial for His servants (Allah does not do what is non-beneficial and harmful; the servant himself creates it).

Baydawi wrote: "Rabbanā li-yuḍillū 'an sabīlika" (the separate clause is an imperative sentence), and in it li-yuḍillū is in the form of a command, and it is a curse upon the disbelievers.

Rabbanā ushdud 'alā amwālihim: "Our Lord, obliterate their wealth (by destroying it) and efface it" (Mujahid). Some scholars said: iṭmās means to transform the form, to distort the shape. Qatadah said that all their wealth, fields and jewels were turned into stone. The forms and shapes remained the same as the original things, but everything had become stone, and some had split into two or three pieces. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz had a bag brought, which contained some remaining items of Pharaoh's people. When he took out an egg, it too was cracked, and a walnut was split, and all the items were stone.

Sudi said: Allah Most High turned all their wealth, trees, fruits, flour and food into stone. This miracle was also one of the nine miracles of Musa.

Wa-shdud 'alā qulūbihim: "and harden their hearts," i.e., make their hearts hard, seal them so that no softness for faith arises in them. Musa made this supplication out of despair regarding them; otherwise Musa had been sent to call them to faith (not to pray that they be kept in denial).

An objection: When Musa knew that they would not believe, then cursing them would be useless.

Answer: The reason for the curse may perhaps be that the nature of faith feels hatred for the enemies of Allah for the sake of Allah (and hatred demands that a curse be made, provided the hatred is not personal but for the sake of Allah). Or Musa may have been commanded to curse them, and in obedience to that command he cursed them. For example, you know that Iblis is cursed by Allah, yet Allah has said: "Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy" (Qur'an 35:6). You curse Satan in obedience to this command.

Fa-lā yu'minū ḥattā yaraw al-'adhāb al-alīm: "So they will not believe until they see the painful punishment" (after death) (Sudi).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 89:

Allah said: "Your supplication has been answered" (addressing Musa and Harun).

Musa was making the supplication while Harun was saying "Amin," so the supplication is attributed to both of them. Baghawi has written that Musa's supplication was answered after forty years.

﴿Fastaqimaa﴾: "So remain steadfast." That is, remain steadfast in the prophethood and the call, and follow My command until the punishment comes upon them.

﴿Wa la tattabi'anna sabilal-ladhina la ya'lamun﴾: "And do not follow the way of those who have no knowledge." That is, do not become hasty about the descent of the punishment as the ignorant people did, or do not lack complete trust in Allah's promise.

And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea. That is, We made them cross and brought them to the other shore. The water split and parted to either side. Moses and his people passed through, walking on dry ground.

Then Pharaoh and his hosts pursued them. Pharaoh and his army also arrived behind the Children of Israel. Tabi'a and atba'a both mean to arrive, to follow from behind, and to catch up with those ahead. Ittaba'a (the form ifti'al) means to follow. Some scholars said: atba'a (the form if'al) and ittaba'a (the form iftiʿal) have the same meaning.

Transgressingly and aggressively: with the intention of injustice and transgression.

Some said: baghyan refers to transgression in speech, and ʿadwan refers to transgression in action. In short, when Pharaoh reached the river's bank with his army, all were afraid to enter it. But Gabriel came (in human form, from the unseen) riding a mare and went into the water at the front, and the horses of the army followed the mare into the river. When the last man had entered the river and the foremost had decided to exit at the other shore, the water suddenly closed back and covered them all.

Until, when drowning overtook him, he said: "I believe that there is no deity except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am among the Muslims." Gabriel immediately filled his mouth with mud, and he died before his repentance was accepted. When the time for accepting repentance had come, the wretch turned away; and when the time for accepting repentance had passed, he made a vehement repentance (which had no result).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 91:

Now? Though you rebelled before and were among the corrupters. (Allah said:) Now (you have come to believe and accept), although before this (throughout your life) you kept disobeying and were among those who spread corruption. You yourself remained misguided, and you also kept leading others away from faith. Baghawi has written, on the authority of Hadrat Ibn Abbas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: When Allah was about to drown Pharaoh (that is, by Allah's command Pharaoh began to drown), he said: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe." Hadrat Jibril said to (the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)): "Muhammad! I wish you had seen that scene, when I was stuffing the sea's mud into his mouth, for I feared that Allah's mercy might reach him (and that his repentance would be accepted before he died)."

Benefit: Jalal al-Din Dawwani says that since Pharaoh had recited the declaration of Tawhid during his lifetime, (his repentance was accepted and) he died a Muslim. Dawwani followed Shaykh Muhyi al-Din Ibn Arabi in this view. Ibn Arabi also holds that Pharaoh died pure.

The truth is that the Shaykh's view contradicts the apparent texts. The many words spoken in his state of intoxication (sukr) are not in accordance with the Shari'ah. The Shaykh's view on Pharaoh is also contrary to the consensus (ijma') of the scholars and does not agree with authentic hadiths.

Dawwani said: Pharaoh's being among the people of Hell is not established by any verse. Wherever a verse warns of the punishment of Hell, it is addressed to the family of Pharaoh, not to Pharaoh himself. Consider that Allah said: "Cause the family of Pharaoh to enter the most severe punishment" (40:46). "He led them to the Fire" (11:98), that is, Pharaoh led his followers into the Fire. "And the evil punishment encompassed the family of Pharaoh" (40:45). This shows that Pharaoh will not be punished for disbelief; rather, since he committed oppression against creation, he will be punished, for the rights of the servants are not forgiven.

I say: Dawwani's argument is baseless. Allah said: "Then he gathered (his people) and proclaimed, saying: I am your lord, the Most High. So Allah seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the former (life)" (79:23-25). Pharaoh gathered everyone and said: "I am your lord, the Most High." Finally Allah seized him and made him an example in this world and the Hereafter (or for the later and earlier generations). From this verse it is clear that Pharaoh will be punished in the Hereafter for disbelief. Another verse records the prayer of Hadrat Musa: "Indeed You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs..." (10:88) etc. At its end Allah says: "Your prayer has been answered" (10:89). From this verse it is understood that Hadrat Musa invoked evil upon Pharaoh and requested that he end in disbelief, and this prayer was accepted; therefore his end was in disbelief. Denying this is denying the verse.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 92:

"So today We shall deliver you in your body (ببدنک), so that you may be a sign for those who come after you." Today We shall cast you upon a high place (so that the flesh is not eaten by fish and the body remains intact in its form), so that you may become a lesson for those who come after you. The word nunajjīka (نُنَجِّيْكَ) is derived from najwah (نجوۃ), which means a high place. Or the meaning is that into the depth of the water where your people were drowned (and their bodies also settled at the bottom), We shall not put your body inside the water as We did theirs, but We shall throw it up above the water. Bi-badanika (ببدنک) means a lifeless corpse, or a complete body, or a naked body. Or bi-badanika may mean that We shall cast you up together with your shirt. A certain shirt of Pharaoh, studded with golden threads and jewels, was famous.

Baghawi has written: When Musa informed his people that Pharaoh had been destroyed, they did not believe it. They said: Pharaoh has not died. To remove their doubt, Allah cast Pharaoh's corpse onto the shore. The corpse was red and small, and appeared to be swollen like an ox (that is, it had bloated). The Children of Israel saw it, recognised him, and confirmed what Musa had told them. Ayah (آيَةً) means a lesson, an admonition, or a sign by which the Oneness of Allah (His power) and the helplessness of the servant are established, even if the servant be a king. The matter was that the notion that Pharaoh would never die had taken firm root in the minds of the Children of Israel; for this reason, even after Musa's announcement, they remained doubtful about Pharaoh's death. Finally, on seeing the corpse lying on the shore, they became certain. Or, "those who come after you" (لِمَنْ خَلْفَكَ) means the people who would come in future times, who, on hearing this event, would take a lesson and refrain from rebellion.

"And indeed many of the people are heedless of Our signs." And many people (that is, the disbelievers) are heedless of Our signs; they do not reflect and do not take a lesson from them.

The Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 93:

And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a goodly abode (that is, We gave them a good place to dwell and a dwelling in which to stay). By "mubawwa'a sidq" is meant a good place, namely Egypt, or Jordan and Palestine. This was the same blessed land which Allah had decreed to grant to Abraham and his descendants. According to Ad-Dahhak, Egypt and Syria are meant.

And We provided them with good things (al-tayyibat).

Yet they did not differ (fa-ma ikhtalafu). That is, the Children of Israel who were present at the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not differ concerning the matter of the final Prophet before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent. They were all agreed that the one who possesses the qualities mentioned in the Torah would be a true Messenger of Allah. They would also give people the good news that the time of the coming of the true Messenger of Allah was near. In battle they would even seek victory over the disbelievers through the means of the final Prophet.

Until knowledge came to them (hatta ja'ahumu al-'ilm). That is, until the one whose qualities they knew came to them. By this is meant the blessed person of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Here "'ilm" carries the sense of "ma'lum" (that which is known), as "khalq" carries the sense of "makhluq" (created thing). Allah has said: "Hadha khalqu Allah" (This is the creation of Allah). Or the meaning is: when the Children of Israel came to know that Muhammad (ﷺ) possessed the very qualities mentioned in the Torah, and they also became acquainted with his miracles, then they split into two groups. Some believed, while the other group, purely out of hostility and envy, refused to accept prophethood.

Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they differed. On the Day of Judgment, Allah will decide the matter over which they dispute and will settle their mutual differences. He will separate the people of truth from the people of falsehood, keep the former safe from punishment, and destroy the latter.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 94:

If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you (O man!), then [the verse says]: if you have doubt about the Qur'an and guidance which We have sent to you through Our Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). (1) [The commentator has taken the address of "kunta" to be every human being, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had no doubt at all. Revelation came to him, the Qur'an was sent down, and the commands of Allah were revealed to him. He possessed a certainty and faith beyond doubt, in which there was no room for any suspicion. Then there is no meaning in seeking confirmation from the People of the Book. Yes, an ignorant polytheist, if he lacks rational and intuitive evidence, needs to seek confirmation from people of knowledge; therefore the address is to the common person.]

So ask those who read the Scriptures before you: ask those who used to read the Book (the Torah and the Gospel) before you. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Dahhak said that the People of the Book referred to are those People of the Book who had accepted faith, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions. That is, ask the believing People of the Book; they will testify that the Book (and Messenger) promised in the Torah and the Gospel is this one. In the narration of stories and the teaching of the basic rulings, it is in agreement with the earlier scriptures.

During the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), there were truly sincere believers and those who inwardly denied and rejected. These two groups existed; a third group also existed, which was caught in doubt between acceptance and rejection, and it is to this group that the verse is addressed.

The verse contains an implicit teaching: that if anyone develops any doubt or suspicion about the truth of the religion, he should turn to the scholars of truth and ask them.

According to some exegetes, the address "kunta" is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the meaning is that, hypothetically, if you were to have doubt; or the purpose of this statement is to keep the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) firm upon faith. This view is supported by the narration reported by 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir that Qatadah said: we have been informed that (after the revelation of this verse) the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: I have no doubt, nor will I ask anyone to remove any doubt.

Some scholars said: the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but the real direction of the address is toward other people. It is the rule of the Arabs (and indeed of the speakers of every language) that in speech they address a specific person, but the intended meaning is not that person himself; rather, others are meant. This style of address has been adopted in various verses. One verse is: "O Prophet! Fear Allah" (Ya ayyuha al-Nabiyyu ittaqi Allah). In this verse the addressee is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but the intended address is to the other believers, because what follows is: "Indeed Allah is ever Aware of what you do" (inna Allaha kana bima ta'malruna khabiran); the verb "ta'malun" is used, which addresses the group. Another verse is: "O Prophet! When you divorce women..." (ya ayyuha al-Nabiyyu idha tallaqtumu al-nisa'), where the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) but the command is given to the believers, and the plural form "tallaqtum" is mentioned.

Al-Farra' said: Allah knew that His Messenger had no doubt, but the style of speech was adopted according to the Arabic idiom. Some people say to their slave: "If you are my slave, then carry out my command; if you are my son, then do this." (Obviously the one giving the command knows that the slave has no doubt about being a slave, nor the son about being a son; yet he still uses the word "if". But this word is not expressing doubt.)

"Indeed the truth has come to you from your Lord": that is, what We have sent down to you is the truth, beyond doubt. Its descent from Allah is established by clear proofs and definitive verses; there is no room for doubt in it.

"So do not be among those who waver": that is, do not be among those who fall into doubt, so that you create wavering in the certainty you already possess and fall into hesitation and perplexity.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 95:

"And do not be among those who denied the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers."

In this verse, as in the previous one, the address is either to those who doubt, or to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while the intended meaning is others. Or the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) himself, but the reason for the address is hypothetical: that is, if on the supposition that he were to deny the signs, he would become among the losers. Or the purpose of the address is to command the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to remain even more firm, to stay steadfast upon his certainty, as in the other verse: "So you shall not be a supporter of the disbelievers" (that is, remain firm in not becoming a helper of the disbelievers).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 96:

Indeed, those against whom the word of your Lord has been fulfilled (i.e., the eternal decree has been established) will not believe, they will not believe.

ḥaqqat (واجب ہوگیا): became binding. The "word of your Lord" refers to the eternal decree that those people will not believe. Mālik, al-Tirmidhī and Abū Dāwūd related, through the narration of Muslim ibn Yasār, that Ḥaḍrat ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was asked about the meaning of the verse: "And when your Lord took from the Children of Ādam, from their loins, their offspring..." He replied: "I myself heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) being asked about the meaning (explanatory and intended) of this verse, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Allah created Ādam, then He passed His right hand over his back and brought forth some of his offspring, and said: I created these for Paradise, and they will do the deeds of the people of Paradise. Then He passed His hand over his back and brought forth some offspring, and said: I created these for the Fire, and they will do the deeds of the people of the Fire." Imām Aḥmad related through Abū Naḍrah, from the Companion Abū ʿAbd Allāh, who said: "I myself heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say that Allah took a handful with His right hand and another handful with His other hand. (About the first he said:) This is for Him, i.e., for Paradise, and this is for Him, i.e., for the Fire, and I do not care (about anyone)."

They will not believe, because the decree of Allah is unbreakable.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 97:

وَلَوْ جَاءَتْهُمْ كُلُّ آيَةٍ — Even if every sign should come to them, (every sign that points to the truth and necessitates faith), because the real cause of faith is the will of Allah, and without His will they cannot believe. So how could they believe?

حَتَّىٰ يَرَوُا الْعَذَابَ الْأَلِيمَ — until they see the painful punishment (with their own eyes). That is, at the time of death in the state of the death-rattle (gharghara), or after death in the graves, or on the Day of Resurrection in Hell. And these are times at which faith brings no benefit, as it brought no benefit to Pharaoh.

﴿Why was there not a town that believed and whose belief benefited it, except the people of Yunus?﴾ Apart from the people of Yunus, why was there no other town that (after witnessing the punishment) believed, and whose belief was beneficial to it? "Town" (qaryah) refers to the people of the town, that is, the inhabitants of those settlements whom Allah destroyed as punishment for denying the Messenger. ﴿Believed﴾ means that they believed before witnessing the punishment, and did not postpone faith until the time of death as Pharaoh did. The purpose of faith being beneficial is that Allah accepted their faith (and averted the punishment that had come upon them).

Abdullah ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) narrates that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah accepts the repentance of His servant as long as the death-rattle has not begun." (Related by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi.)

Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) narrates that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah surely forgives His servant as long as the veil is not drawn." The Companions asked: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the veil?" He said: "Dying in a state of shirk." (Related by Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi in Kitab al-Ba'th wa'l-Nushur.)

"Lawla" is a particle of exhortation (urging and stirring to action). It carries the meaning of negation, so ﴿illa qawma Yunus﴾ is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), meaning that the people of Yunus are excluded. The sense is that the people of Yunus are the exception. They believed at the time of witnessing the (worldly) punishment, and their faith benefited them (Allah accepted their repentance), and they were protected from the punishment of the Hereafter. (However, the people of Yunus believed before the death-rattle and before witnessing the punishment of the Hereafter.)

﴿Lamma amanu﴾: when they believed, that is, when they believed while still in a state of free choice. Then We accepted their faith. Ibn Mardawayh, on the authority of Aisha, cites the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) under this verse, that when they believed, they made this supplication:

﴿We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world﴾, and ﴿We gave them enjoyment for a time﴾: that is, for a specified appointed time in this world. The appointed time refers to the time of death, which was known to Allah.

Baghawi wrote: the meaning of this verse is that no town believed after witnessing the punishment and derived benefit from its faith in that state, except the people of Yunus. They benefited from believing at such a time.

On this point, scholars hold two opinions. One group says that the people of Yunus saw the punishment with their own eyes and believed after that. The other group says that they saw only the signs of the punishment, not the punishment itself. The first opinion is that of most scholars, because Allah said ﴿We removed from them the punishment of disgrace﴾, and the removal of punishment occurs only after it has taken place.

The implication of Baghawi's statement is that the faith of someone in the state of the worldly punishment (which Baghawi called the state of "ba's," severe calamity) is not acceptable. In the state of ba's, only the faith of the people of Yunus was accepted, and no one else's was.

The correct view is that the ﴿painful punishment﴾ in the verse refers to the punishment of the Hereafter, which appears in the form of the angel of death before the deceased at the time of death. Faith after witnessing this punishment is not acceptable (whereas faith after witnessing a worldly punishment is acceptable). Consider: on the day of Badr, the disbelievers suffered a worldly punishment in the form of killing and captivity. Those disbelievers who survived that battle and later believed had their faith accepted. The same happened to the people of Yunus. They believed before witnessing the punishment of the Hereafter, even though they had seen the worldly punishment with their own eyes and believed after seeing it. Their faith was still accepted, and Allah removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the worldly life.

As for Pharaoh's faith not being accepted, the reason is either that he believed in the state of the death-rattle at the time of death, which is unacceptable, or that although he expressed faith verbally, (Allah knew that) he did not believe in his heart. Moses had invoked a curse upon him, and his curse was accepted, so Pharaoh was not one who would believe sincerely. It had become the habit of Pharaoh and his people that whenever a punishment befell them, they would say: "Moses, invoke your Lord to remove this punishment from us. If you have it removed, we will believe in you and let the Children of Israel go with you." But when Allah removed the punishment for a fixed period, they broke their covenant and went back on their promise. Thus it is possible that even at the last time Pharaoh did not believe sincerely, and only acknowledged it verbally.

The question of whether faith is accepted in the state of the death-rattle has been discussed by us under the commentary on the verse of Surah al-Nisa: ﴿Repentance is only accepted by Allah from those who do evil in ignorance﴾ (4:17), and we have explained it there.

**The Story of Prophet Yunus (peace be upon him)**

Baghawi has narrated the following on the authority of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Wahb ibn Munabbih and others.

The people of Yunus lived in Nineveh, in the region of Mosul. Allah appointed Yunus to guide them. Yunus invited them to faith, but they refused to accept it. Allah commanded Yunus: "Tell them that a punishment will come upon them at dawn in three days." Yunus informed them. The people said: "Experience has shown that this man has never lied. So wait and see! If he stays with you tonight, know that nothing will happen in the morning. But if he does not stay with you at night, know that the punishment will surely come in the morning." In the middle of the night, Yunus went out from among the people. When morning came, the punishment appeared one mile above their heads. Wahb said: the punishment came like a black cloud, emitting thick smoke, then descended and covered the city, so that the roofs of the houses became black. Seeing this, the people became certain that they would perish. They searched for Yunus but could not find him anywhere. Finally, Allah put into their hearts the idea of repentance, and the old and young, men and women, and animals all gathered in the open ground outside the city. Everyone put on sackcloth, and they began to repent and to affirm their faith with a sincere intention. Each mother had been separated from her child, and even the young of the animals had been separated from their mothers. Because of this separation, the children of humans and animals began to cry out, and the mothers too, under the influence of love, began to cry (a great wailing arose). In anguish they all cried out and pleaded before Allah. At last Allah had mercy on them, answered their supplication, and removed the punishment that had overshadowed them. This event took place on the 10th of Muharram.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh have narrated the account of Qatadah, who said: "It has been told to us that the people of Yunus lived at Nineveh, in the region of Mosul." This account adds that when Allah witnessed the sincerity of their hearts and knew their repentance and remorse, He removed the punishment, although the punishment had hung over their heads, and only one mile remained.

Ibn Abi Hatim has narrated from Ali that the repentance of the people of Yunus was accepted on the day of Ashura. Yunus went out of the town and waited for the punishment to descend and the people to perish. But when he saw that the punishment did not come, (according to the custom of that time, if anyone lied without proof, he would be put to death), Yunus said: "I told my people a lie (that is, my lie has been proven), so how can I return to them?" Thinking this, he departed, angry with his people and displeased with his Lord. When he reached the river, some people were boarding a boat. They recognized him and took him aboard without a fare. When the boat carried him into the middle of the sea, it stopped; it could neither move forward nor go back. The boatmen said: "There must be a specific reason for the boat to be stuck." Yunus said: "I know the reason. There is a great sinner aboard." The people asked: "Who is he?" Yunus said: "I am. Throw me into the river." The people said: "Unless we have a clear reason, we will not throw you." Finally they cast lots, and three times Yunus's name came up. Yunus said: "Either you throw me into the water, or you will all perish." Reluctantly, the boatmen threw him overboard. As soon as he was thrown, the boat set off. Near the bottom of the boat, a fish was waiting with open mouth for Allah's command. As soon as Yunus fell into the water, the fish took him into its mouth.

It is also reported that Allah commanded a great fish, and it turned toward the boat. The boatmen saw it approaching with its mouth open, as large as a mountain, and they sensed that it was seeking someone inside the boat. As soon as Yunus saw this, he leapt into the water (and the fish caught him).

Ibn Abbas said that Yunus went out angry with his people and arrived at the Mediterranean Sea. There a ship full of passengers was standing. He boarded it. When the ship set sail and reached the middle of the sea, it stopped and stood still. It was about to sink with all on board. The sailors said: "There is a sinful man or a runaway slave aboard our ship, which is why it has stopped. Our custom in such a case is to cast lots. The one whose name comes out is thrown into the sea (and then the ship sails on). Drowning one man is better than the whole ship being lost with its passengers." Accordingly, they cast lots three times, and each time Yunus's name came out. Yunus immediately stood up and said: "I am the sinful man and the runaway slave." Then he threw himself into the sea. At once a fish swallowed him, and then a larger fish came and swallowed that fish. Allah commanded the fish that not the slightest harm should come to Yunus: "I have made your belly a prison for him, not made him your food." In Ibn Abbas's narration, it is said that the fish was called out: "We have not made Yunus your provision, but have made your belly a place of his protection and a house of worship."

It is also reported that before the lots were cast, Yunus stood up and said: "I am the sinner, the runaway slave." The sailors asked: "Who are you?" He said: "Yunus son of Matta." The people recognized him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we will not throw you, but we will cast lots." Lots were cast, Yunus's name came out, and he threw himself into the water.

Ibn Mas'ud said: the fish that swallowed him took him down to the depths of the seventh earth, and he remained in the fish's belly for forty nights. There he heard the sound of the pebbles glorifying Allah, and in the darkness he cried out: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ (21:87). Allah answered his supplication, and by Allah's command the fish brought him and threw him onto the shore of the sea. At that time his condition was like a chick whose feathers had been plucked. Immediately Allah caused a gourd tree to grow, under whose shade he rested, and He appointed a mountain goat (or a wild goat) to him, and he drank its milk. When the tree dried up, Yunus wept over the tree. Allah sent a revelation: "You wept over a tree that dried up, but you did not weep for the hundred thousand or more people, and you wanted to have them destroyed." From there Yunus set out and met a slave who was herding animals. He asked him: "Slave, who are you?" He said: "I am of the people of Yunus." The Prophet said: "When you go to your people, tell them that I met Yunus." The slave said: "You know that if I have no witnesses, I will be put to death (for giving false information)." Yunus said: "This piece of land and this tree will testify for you." The slave said: "Then instruct them to testify." Yunus said: "When this slave comes to you, both of you should testify on his behalf." The land and the tree said: "Very well." The slave went and informed his king that he had met Yunus. The king ordered that the slave be put to death. The slave said: "I have witnesses to the truth of this; send someone with me." So the slave took people with him to that place and to that tree, and said: "I ask you both by Allah: did Yunus make you witnesses?" They both said: "Yes." Upon hearing this, the people were terrified and returned, and they told the king that the tree and the land had testified for the slave. The king took the slave by the hand, seated him in his own place, and said: "You are more entitled to this place than I am." The slave administered their affairs for forty years.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 10, verse 99:

﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on the earth would have believed, all of them entirely.﴾ (O Muhammad (ﷺ)!) If your Lord had willed, all those who are on the earth would have come to faith together, every one of them. None would have remained without faith, and no one would have differed concerning faith. All of them would have agreed upon belief.

The Qadariyyah sect holds that Allah wishes all people to become believers, but people themselves, by their own choice, do not wish to believe. (According to this sect, there is no difference between mashi'ah (will) and ridha (pleasure); to "will" means to "approve".) The Ash'ariyyah say that Allah does approve of everyone's faith, but He does not will that all should become believers. A deviation from the pleasure of Allah is possible, but a deviation from His will is not possible. According to the Qadariyyah, what is ridha is itself mashi'ah; ridha is general, mashi'ah is also general; it is possible to act contrary to ridha, and it does happen; it is also possible to act contrary to mashi'ah, and it does happen. The verse shows that Allah did not will to make all people believers; had His will been so, they would all have become believers. (Yes, it is pleasing to Him that all should believe.) The Qadariyyah answered this by saying that mashi'ah in the verse means compelling will (mashi'ah mujbirah), and that it is not possible to act against a compelling divine will. (Therefore, there is no compelling will of Allah that all should become believers.) But this additional condition is contrary to the apparent meaning.

﴿Will you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ (O Muhammad (ﷺ)!) Would you compel people to become believers when Allah has not willed it? The interrogative is a denial, and the placing of the pronoun ANTA before the verb TUKRIHU indicates that, since Allah has not willed it, the existence of such a thing is impossible. It cannot be attained even by compulsion, let alone by encouragement. The matter is this: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was extremely eager that all people should become believers... (Yet) his task was only to give encouragement; he had no authority to compel. And that which cannot be accomplished even by compulsion, how can it be accomplished by mere encouragement? Thus Allah made it clear that whoever is destined for felicity will believe, and whoever is wretched in the knowledge of Allah cannot believe; so do not be concerned about them. Thus in this verse there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Verse 10:100: "And it is not for any soul to believe except by the permission of Allah." No soul has the power to believe without the will and enabling grace (tawfiq) of Allah.

"And He places defilement upon those who do not reason." Rijs (defilement) here means punishment, or deprivation of Allah's help, since this deprivation is itself the cause of punishment. "Not reasoning" means failing to distinguish between truth and falsehood. That is, because seals have been placed upon the hearts of the disbelievers, and Allah does not will that they be able to distinguish truth from falsehood, therefore they have no ability to tell truth from falsehood.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 101:

Say: "Look at what is in the heavens and the earth." (O Muhammad (ﷺ)!) Tell them: look, reflect, and think! What wondrous signs there are in the heavens and the earth: the moon, the sun, the stars, their structure and their regular motion, the mountains and their firmness, the seas, the rivers, the trees, and the world of plants and animals. In all these things the power and craftsmanship of a Creator who is capable, wise and one is shining forth. Through them the greatness of His Being and the perfection of His attributes are being manifested.

﴿And of what use are the signs and the warners to a people who do not believe?﴾ That is, to a people who, in the knowledge and by the will of Allah, are not going to believe, what benefit are the signs (which create knowledge and certainty) and the warners (the prophets and lessons that admonish)?

In "ma tughni", the word "ma" is either a negation (there is no benefit) or an interrogative of denial (what benefit?).

"An-nudhur" is the plural of "nadhir", meaning warners. It refers to the messengers of Allah (who warn of the punishment for disobedience to Allah) and to other lesson-giving things, such as old age (which is a sign of decline and death) and the death of companions (which is enough to convince a person of his own death and to frighten him). Since faith is purely a gift from Allah (its attainment depends upon His will), it is said that those who will not believe, that is, whose faith has not been decreed in Allah's knowledge and will, will not believe even on seeing a sign or hearing a warning.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 102:

Fa-hal yantazirna illa mithla ayyam al-ladhina khalaw min qablihim. So they (i.e., the polytheists of Makkah) are not waiting except for the like of the events and calamities that befell the disbelievers who passed before them.

Qatadah said: That is, the like of the punishment of Allah that came upon the people of Nuh, 'Ad and Thamud.

In Arabic idiom, the word ayyam (days) is used to mean both punishment and blessings. Allah said: ﴿And remind them of the Days of Allah﴾ (Ibrahim 14:5). Thus, whatever good or calamity comes upon human beings is called ayyam.

Qul fa-intazirru inni ma'akum mina al-muntazirin. Say (O Muhammad ﷺ): "Wait, then, and I am with you among those who wait." That is, let you wait for my destruction; I too am waiting along with you among those who wait (for your destruction).

Then We save Our messengers and those who believe. Thus it is incumbent upon Us: We save the believers. (Note: this is the translation of the passage as given.)

Wait, I must correct that: I should not add notes. Here is the faithful translation only:

Then We save Our messengers and those who believed. (In the past, when a people rejected and were destroyed, We would destroy the disbelievers and deniers, and save Our prophets and those who believed in them. This is the account of what happened in the past, that this was Our practice in earlier times.)

Thus, as is Our due, We shall save the believers. In the same way (that is, as with the earlier prophets), We will save the believers. This is Our promise, binding upon Us. The meaning is this: just as We saved the earlier prophets and believers, so too at the time of the descent of punishment, We will save Muhammad (ﷺ) and those who believe in him, and this salvation is binding upon Us according to Our promise.

Say, [O Prophet]: "O people! (that is, O people of Makkah), if you are in doubt about my religion (its truth)..."

The people of Makkah found prophethood something very difficult to comprehend, yet, seeing the signs, they were compelled to accept it; but because of their innate wretchedness they remained in doubt and hesitation. (That is, they were compelled to accept on seeing the signs, and their natural perversity did not allow tranquility to settle in their hearts.)

﴿Then I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah⦆ — that is, I do not worship those (stone idols) that you worship besides Allah.

﴿But I worship Allah, who causes you to die⦆ — that is, who gives you life, then gives you death, and who creates whatever He wills and in whatever manner He wills. (Although the creation of both death and life is intended, the mention of death alone is made to instill a warning.) The words "fa-la a'budu" are not the response (jaza') to "in kuntum" but stand in its place; the cause has been placed in the position of the effect. The essence of the statement is this: if you have doubt about the truth of my religion, then reflect on my religion and remove that doubt. Look! I do not worship those stones, which hold neither benefit nor harm, but I worship the God who is the Creator, the Powerful, and the Master of benefit and harm.

﴿And I have been commanded to be among the believers⦆ — that is, rational proofs and the divine scriptures command that I be a believer and remain a man of faith.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 105:

"And [it is also commanded]: Set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth (hanifa), and do not be among the polytheists."

It has also been commanded: keep your orientation toward this religion (pure monotheism), turning away from every other religion, and by no means be among the polytheists. That is, you have also been commanded to remain firm in faith, to maintain steadfastness in religion, to perform the obligations with diligence, and to refrain from wrongdoing. (Thus, the phrase "aqimu wajhaka lil-ladhina" means the fulfilment of all obligations and abstention from prohibited things.) Or, "iqamat wajh" may mean performing the prayer while facing the qiblah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 106:

Wa la tad'u min dūnillāhi mā lā yanfa'uka wa lā yadurruka: "And do not invoke, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit you nor harm you" (i.e., do not worship, besides Allah, such things as can neither benefit you if you worship them nor harm you if you abandon their worship) (1). [That is, do not worship any creature besides Allah. The word "invoke" here means worship, because creatures have no power to benefit or harm.] This sentence is joined to, and is an explanation of, "la takūnanna mina al-mushrikīn" (so do not be among the polytheists).

This is a fact, and it is confirmed by both rational and transmitted evidence: if this religion of Islam is viewed with an impartial eye and considered with careful reflection, the soundness of the religion becomes established, and every doubt against the religion itself dispels.

Fa-in fa'alta fa-innaka idhan mina al-ẓālimīn: "And if (hypothetically) you were to do so, then certainly you would, in that case, be among the wrongdoers." That is, if you were to worship something that is neither beneficial nor harmful, then undoubtedly in that case you would be acting unjustly (a zālim), since you would be making the focus of your worship a being that is not fit to be worshipped.

Sayyid Qutb, Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation), commentary on Surah 10, verse 107:

﴿And if Allah should touch you with harm, there is none to remove it except Him; and if He should intend for you good, there is none to repel His bounty.﴾

"Mass" means to reach or to afflict. "Darr" means illness, hardship, or calamity. "Fa la kashifa lahu" means there is no one to remove it. (Kashf literally means to uncover; here it means to remove or repel.) "Khayr" means good, both of this world and of the Hereafter. Harm and good both occur by Allah's will, but in this place the use of the word "mass" with "darr" and the word "irada" (intention) with "khayr" probably points to the fact that Allah's real purpose is to bestow good, and inflicting harm is not His primary aim. The addition of the word "fadl" (bounty) in "li-fadlihi," instead of a plain pronoun, shows that what Allah bestows, He bestows out of His mercy, and no one has any right over it.

﴿He afflicts with it whom He wills of His servants, and He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ That is, He afflicts with hardship and grants ease to whomever among His servants He wills. Whether it is good or evil, everything is caused by Allah alone, to whom He wills. Therefore, it is incumbent upon you to be seekers of good through obedience, but do not place your trust in your obedience, and do not despair of forgiveness either; rather, fear punishment (and hope for mercy). Abu Nu'aym, through the narration of Hazrat Ali, has written that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Allah sent a revelation to one of the Prophets among the Israelite prophets, that he should tell those among his community who were obedient: do not place your trust in your deeds. On the Day of Judgment, when I stand the servants up for reckoning, whomever I wish to punish, I will punish (and I will take his reckoning with close scrutiny), and tell the sinners of my community not to destroy themselves (that is, do not despair). If I wish, I will forgive great sins, and I will not mind.

By revealing the above verses, Allah has closed the path of fearing or hoping in anyone other than Himself.

Allah is Forgiving and Merciful, meaning His mercy prevails over His wrath.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 10, verse 108:

﴿Say: O mankind, the truth has certainly come to you from your Lord.﴾ (O Muhammad (ﷺ)!) Say: O people! There has come to you from your Lord the correct and true knowledge.

Al-Haqq (the truth) means correct knowledge, that is, the oneness of Allah, His attributes, and the conditions of the origin and the return, which have been made clear in the Qur'an and through the words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Now no excuse of ignorance remains for anyone.

Or, by al-Haqq is meant that (the Qur'an or the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)) whose truth has been established through its inimitability (i'jaz), and so no excuse remains for anyone.

﴿So whoever is guided⦆ Whoever is guided now, that is, believes in this knowledge and walks on the path it shows.

﴿then he is guided only for his own self⦆ He will be guided for his own benefit (that is, its benefit returns to him himself).

﴿And whoever goes astray⦆ And whoever strays from the path of truth, that is, denies it.

﴿then he goes astray only to its detriment⦆ Then the harm of his straying falls upon his own self.

﴿And I am not a guardian over you⦆ I am not responsible for you. It is not my duty over your affairs, such that I should be held accountable for your straying.

This is the conclusion of the discourse, and it is in harmony with the beginning of the surah. These final words also suit the themes of the entire surah. The manner of the Holy Qur'an is precisely this: it presents its message through a balanced portrayal. Sadaqa Allahu al-'Azim!
